Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 47, verse 1–11 (part 3 of 3):

It is apparent that His saying: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for His saying: ﴿then bind them firmly﴾, because the striking of necks has already been made conditional on binding them firmly at the time of overpowering (al-ithkhan). It is not possible for it to be made conditional by another limit, since the two limits would conflict, unless the second is explanatory of the first and emphasizing it. Then it is permissible, because the binding of captives happens only until the war lays down its burdens. This applies when we interpret it as the disappearance of the strength of the unbelievers who are engaged at that time, and "the war" here means that which occurs at the time the believers meet the unbelievers. It is also permissible that the limited element be omitted and understood from the meaning, the estimate being: the ruling is that until the war lays down its burdens, meaning that no strength remains for them. Or, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, it is a metaphor meaning "until the Day of Resurrection," i.e., do that always. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is 'until' attached?" I say: it must be attached either to the striking and binding, or to the granting of favour and ransom. The meaning according to both attachments, in the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, is that they continue in this state forever until there is a war with the polytheists, and that is when they have no strength left. It was also said: when Jesus son of Mary descends. And according to Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, it is attached to striking and binding. The meaning is: they are killed and taken captive until the kind of war lays down its burdens, and that is until the polytheists have no strength left. If it is attached to granting favour and ransom, the meaning is: they are granted favour and ransomed until the war of Badr lays down its burdens, until the granting of favour and ransom is taken, meaning: by setting them free from killing and enslaving them, that is, by allowing them to remain under the imposition of the jizyah by being among the People of the Covenant (dhimmah), and by the punishment that they be ransomed in exchange for the captives of the polytheists among the captives of the Muslims. Al-Tahawi narrated this as the school of Abu Hanifah, but the well-known view is that he does not permit their ransom with wealth or otherwise, out of fear that they would return as enemies to the Muslims. (That) i.e., the matter is that, if they do it.

﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾: i.e., He would have punished them with some of the causes of destruction, such as a sinking into the earth, or a quake, or a violent wind, or drowning, or a overwhelming death.

﴿But that He may test﴾: i.e., but He commanded you to fight so that He may test some of you, namely the believers, by means of others, namely the unbelievers, by having them strive and endure, and having the unbelievers be hastened at their hands with some of the punishment due to them. Al-Jumhur read qatalu (qaatalu), with a fatha on the qaf and ta, without an alif; Qatadah, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read qutilu, in the passive, with a light ta; Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Isa and al-Jahdari likewise. 'Ali read: fa-lan yudalla, in the passive, their deeds being the subject, in the nominative. It was also read: yadilla, with a fatha on the ya, from dalla, their deeds being in the nominative.

﴿He will guide them﴾: i.e., to the path of Paradise. Mujahid said: the people of Paradise will find their way to their dwellings in it without error, for they were its inhabitants since they were created, and they will not be confused about it. 'Iyad narrated from Abu 'Amr: wa-yudkhilhumu (and He will admit them). And "yawma yajma'kum li-yawm al-jam'" and "innama nut'imukum" with the consonant of the word's lam pronounced with sukun.

﴿He made it known to them﴾: From Muqatil: the angel who was assigned to guard his deeds in this world walks before him and informs him of everything God has given him. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid and Qatadah said: its meaning is that He made them recognize it, i.e., made them know their abodes in it. In a hadith: "One of you is more knowledgeable of his abode in Paradise than of his abode in this world." It was also said: He named it for them and marked each dwelling with its owner, and this is a kind of making known. It is said: "He knew the house and marked its boundaries," i.e., he delimited it, so each person's paradise is set apart from others. And al-'Urf and al-Urf mean boundaries. It was also said: He honored it for them, raised it and elevated it, and this is from the a'raf, which are the mountains and what resembles them. Mawrij and others said: He made it fragrant, derived from al-'arf, and from it: "a food that is 'arrafa," i.e., made fragrant, as one says "'arrafa al-qidr," meaning he made the pot fragrant with salt and seasoning.

﴿If you help God﴾: i.e., His religion; (He will help you): i.e., against your enemies, by creating strength in you and other such means of knowledge.

﴿And make your feet firm﴾: i.e., in the places of war, or upon the path of Islam. Al-Jumhur read wa-yuthabbit (with shaddah), and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read it without shaddah.

﴿Then, destruction for them﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a distance (from good) for them; Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi: grief for them; al-Hasan: cursing; Ibn Zayd: wretchedness; al-Dahhak: humiliation; and al-Naqqash related: ugliness. (And those who disbelieved): is a subject (mubtada'), and the fa' enters into the predicate of the subject, its estimate being: fa-ta'isahumu Allah ta'san (so God causes them to stumble with a stumbling). So ta'san is in the accusative by a hidden verb, and for this reason the verb "and He made their deeds go astray" is conjoined to it. It is also permissible that alladhina be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by His saying "then, destruction for them," as you say "Zaydan, jad'an lahu." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "On what is His saying 'and He made their deeds go astray' conjoined?" I say: on the verb that governed ta'san, because the meaning is: "he said ta'san for them" or "he decreed ta'san for them," and ta'san lahum is the opposite of la'an lahu. End quote. And it is better to supply a verb from the same root as the verbal noun, because this indicates what was omitted. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means in this world killing, and in the Hereafter falling headlong into the Fire. End quote. In His saying "fa-ta'san lahum," i.e., destruction, with a particle that strengthens the hearts of the believers, since He gave them firmness, and gave the unbelievers destruction and stumbling.

﴿That is because they hated what God revealed﴾: it includes what was revealed of the Qur'an in clarifying monotheism, mentioning resurrection, the obligatory duties and limits, and other things the Qur'an contains. (So He made their deeds fruitless): i.e., He made them among the deeds which do not grow and are not counted.

﴿God destroyed them utterly﴾: i.e., He ruined for them what they were specially attached to of their own selves, their children and their wealth, and all that belonged to them and to the unbelievers like them. That is the outcome and the destruction indicated by "destroyed" and the ruin, because destruction indicates it; or the sunnah, by His saying, "the sunnah of God concerning those who passed before." The first interpretation is the preferred one, because the outcome is stated explicitly, so the pronoun refers back to what is spoken, and what follows is the content of the saying. (That is because): an inceptive and predicate, and the indication of "that" refers, in the choice of a group, to the victory, and to the destruction, as He said: ﴿and for the unbelievers there are similar ones﴾. He said that the destruction which was made for the unbelievers at the hands of the believers is because God is their protector (mawla), i.e., their helper and supporter, and because the unbelievers have no helper, since they took gods that neither benefit nor harm, and abandoned the worship of Him who benefits and harms, namely God, exalted is He.

Qatadah said: this verse was revealed on the day of Uhud, and from it the Messenger of God ﷺ took his reply to Abu Sufyan when he said: "Say: God is our Protector, and you have no protector," when the polytheists said: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 47, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 3)**

(Surat al-Qital, forty verses, Madani.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

(p-70) ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, He will absolve them of their misdeeds and set right their state.﴾ ﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, while those who believe follow the truth from their Lord. Thus Allah sets forth their parables for mankind.﴾ ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, bind them firmly. Then either grant them release or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens. That is the case. Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them Himself, but He tests some of you by means of others. As for those who are slain in the way of Allah, He will not let their deeds go astray.﴾ ﴿He will guide them and set right their state.﴾ ﴿And He will admit them to the Garden, which He has made known to them.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you and make your feet firm.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is ruin, and He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah has sent down, so He has nullified their deeds.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and there await the disbelievers similar things.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾

(This surah is Madani according to the majority. Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said it is Makki. Ibn Atiyyah said it is Madani by consensus, but that is not as he said. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that it is Madani except for one verse, which was revealed after his Hajj, when he left Makkah and began looking towards the House. That verse is: "And how many a town..." The connection between its beginning and the end of what precedes it is very clear.)

**Linguistic notes**

*al-bal* (the mind, the thought): it means *al-fikr* (reflection). One says, "such-and-such occurred to my mind" (*kadha*). It is not made dual or plural, though the irregular plural *balat* has been reported.

*ta'asa* (to stumble and fall): *ta'isa* with a fatha on the ʿayn, *ta'san*, is the opposite of *tanaʿʿush* (to be raised up), and Allah makes one *ta'isa*. Mujammi' ibn Hilal said:

*"She says, having separated me from her husband: 'You have stumbled, as you made me stumble, O Mujammiʿ.'"*

Some, among them Amr ibn Shumayl and Abu al-Haytham, said *ta'iba* with a kasra on the ʿayn. From Abu Ubaydah: *ta'isahu Allah* and *at'asahu Allah* belong to the pattern *fa'ila* and *af'ala*. Ibn as-Sikkit said: *at-ta's* is to be dragged upon the face, and *an-naks* is to be dragged upon the head. He also said, and Tha'lab with him, that *at-ta's* is destruction. Al-Aʿsha said:

*"With a she-camel that is pale-hued, sturdy, and swift, when she stumbles, then 'ruin' is more fitting for her than my saying 'ʿaʿa'."*

*asin* (stagnant, foul-smelling water): water whose smell has changed. The verb is *yaʾsinu* and *yaʾsunu*. Tha'lab mentioned it in *al-Fasih*. The verbal noun is *usun* and *asin* with a kasra on the sin. *Yaʾsanu* with a fatha is a dialect form, reported by al-Yazidi. *Asina ar-rajul*, with a kasra only, means that a man entered a well, was struck by a smell from the well, and fainted or became dizzy. The poet said:

*"I shall leave the opponent pale, his fingertips yellowed, swaying in the wind like one who has been overcome by the well's stench."*

*ashrat* (signs, indications): the singular is *shart*, with a sukun or a fatha on the raʾ. Abu al-Aswad said:

*"If you have resolved to sever our bond, then the signs of its beginning have already appeared."*

*Ashrata ar-rajul nafsahu* means he obliged himself to certain duties. Aws ibn Hajar said:

*"So he bound himself to them, while he was a man of firm grip, and he cast himself upon his means and relied on them."*

*al-ʿasal* (honey) is well known. ʿAsal ibn Dhakwan was an early grammarian. *al-miʿa* (intestines): it is a maqsur noun whose alif is converted from a ya', as shown by its dual *miʿayan*, with the alif changed to ya'. *Al-miʿa* is what is in the belly of the intestines.

*al-qufl* (lock) is well known, and its root meaning is dryness and hardness. *Al-qufl* and *al-qafil* are wood that has dried up. *Al-qafil* is also a plant, and it is also a whip. *Aqfalahu as-sawm* means fasting dried him out. Al-Jawhari said this.

*ayifan* and *a'nifan* (just now): both are active participles, and their verb is not used. The verb that is used is *i'tanafa*. Both mean "beginning" (*mubtadiʾan*). Interpreting them as "the Hour" is an interpretation of meaning. Az-Zajjaj said: it derives from *istanaftu ash-shayʾ*, meaning I began the thing.

*fa-awla lahum*: the author of *as-Sihah* said: the Arabs' saying *awla laka* is a threat and warning, and from it is the poet's line:

*"Awla, then awla, then awla, and is there for the house any return from its milk?"*

End of his words. They differed over whether *awla* is a noun or a verb. Al-Asmaʿi held that it means that which destruction approaches, i.e., it came near to him. He recited:

*"They became hostile between the two front-ones, and it was near that it would exceed three."*

That is, it came near to exceeding. Tha'lab said: no one has said anything better about *awla* than what al-Asmaʿi said. Al-Mubarrad said: it is said to one who is about to perish. It is reported that a Bedouin would constantly shoot at game, which would escape from him, so he would say, "Awla laka (woe to you), you shot at game." He came near to hitting it, then it escaped from him. He said:

*"Had awla fed the people their game, but awla leaves the people hungry."*

Most scholars hold that it is a noun. It is said to be derived from *al-wali*, which is nearness, as the poet said:

*"Layla burdens me, though her nearness has gone far, and the vicissitudes have returned between us."*

Al-Jurjani said: it is what has been transformed from *al-waylu* (woe), so it is *afʿal* from it, but there is inversion in it.

*ad-dighn* and *ad-daghina* (rancour, grudge): the hatred. ʿAmr ibn Kulthum said:

*"Rancour after rancour spreads against you, and the hidden disease comes out."*

One says *daghina* with a kasra, and *tadaghana al-qawm* and *adghanu* mean they harboured grudges. *Daghina ʿalayhi* means he bore a grudge against him. *Adghanta as-sabiyya* means you took the child under your arm. Al-Ahmar recited:

*"As if he were a rancorous one who hides a child."*

Ibn Muqbil said:

*"And I did not rancorously hide my weapon at its battle."*

*Faras daghin* is a horse that does not give what it has of running except under beating. The root of the word is from *ad-dighn*, which is twisting and bending in the legs of an animal, a spear, and everything. Bishr said:

*"Like the one with bent legs walking in the alley."*

Al-Layth recited:

*"Indeed my young girl, from the spears' well-knotted (ones), the straightening did not increase her except rancour."*

Hatred in the heart is likened to it. Qutrub said:

*"And al-Layth made hostility more hidden."*

The poet said:

*"Say to the son of Hind: I did not intend by my speech anything except that friendship has grown and hostility has been built up."*

*laḥantu lahu*, with a fatha on the ḥa': *alḥanu laḥnan*. I said to him a statement which he understands from you and which is hidden from others. *Laḥina-hu* with a kasra means he understood it. *Alḥanahu* means he made him understand. *Alḥantuhu anā iyyāhu* and *lāḥantu an-nās* mean I outwitted people. The poet said:

*"Speech that is correct and that subtly alludes, and the best speech is that which is allusive."*

Al-Qattal al-Kilabi said:

*"And indeed I spoke to you so that you would understand, and I alluded in an allusion that is not doubtful."*

It is said that *laḥn al-qawl* means departing from what is correct, and it is taken from *al-laḥn* in grammar (i.e., error in inflection). *Wataraha* means he diminished it, taken from *adh-dhahl* (enmity). It is said it is taken from *al-watr*, which is singular.

(p-72) ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, He has rendered their deeds void.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, He has absolved them of their misdeeds and set right their state.﴾ ﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, while those who believe follow the truth from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Thus Allah sets forth their parables for mankind.﴾ ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, bind them firmly. Then either grant them release or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens.﴾ ﴿That is the case. Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them Himself, but He tests some of you by means of others. As for those who are slain in the way of Allah, He will not let their deeds go astray.﴾ ﴿He will guide them and set right their state.﴾ ﴿And He will admit them to the Garden, which He has made known to them.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you and make your feet firm.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is ruin, and He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah has sent down, so He has nullified their deeds.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ ﴿Allah destroyed them, and there await the disbelievers similar things.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾

This surah is Madani according to the majority. Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said it is Makki. Ibn Atiyyah said it is Madani by consensus, but that is not as he said. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that it is Madani except for one verse, which was revealed after his Hajj, when he left Makkah and began looking towards the House. That verse is: "And how many a town..." The connection between its beginning and the end of what precedes it is very clear.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 47, verses 1–11 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾: that is, they turned away from entering Islam, or they barred others from it. They are the people of Makkah who expelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas said: they are the ones who gave food [to the Quraysh] on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: they were twelve men from among the polytheists, who barred people from Islam and commanded them to disbelieve. It was also said: they are the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), who barred those among them and others who wished to enter Islam. Al-Dahhak said: "the way of Allah" means the House of Allah, preventing those who seek it, and it is general to everyone who disbelieves and bars [others].

﴿He has made their deeds go astray﴾: that is, He has destroyed them, since no good or benefit came from them, but only pure harm. It was also said: this verse was revealed at Badr, and that the reference in His words "He has made their deeds go astray" is to the agreement they made during their journey to Badr. It was also said: the intended "deeds" are their good acts in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyya), such as maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, and the like, and the wording covers all of that.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: they are the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah). Muqatil said: they are some people from Quraysh. It was also said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. It was also said: the verse is general, and even if the cause of revelation is specific to the two groups, the wording encompasses every disbeliever and every believer.

﴿And believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾: singling him out from among what must be believed in is an exalting of the Messenger's station and an informing that faith is neither valid nor complete except through him. This is emphasised by the parenthetical clause, which is: ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾. It was said: "and it is the truth" abrogates what came before it, and abrogation (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) does not apply to it. The majority of readers recite "nuzzila" in the passive voice; Zayd ibn Ali and Ibn Miqsam recite "nazzala" in the active voice; al-A'mash recites "unzila," with the hamza making it transitive, in the passive voice. It was also read as "nazala," in the triliteral form.

﴿He will remit their misdeeds and set right their state﴾: that is, their condition (ḥāl), said Qatada; their affairs (sha'n), said Mujahid; their matter (amr), said Ibn Abbas. The literal meaning of the word "bal" (state of mind, concern) is "thought," and the place where a person's attention lies is the heart. When that is made right, his condition is made right, so the wording points to the soundness of their creed, and the rest of their condition follows from it.

﴿That﴾: a reference to what was done to the disbelievers, namely the misguiding of their deeds, and to the believers, namely the remission of their misdeeds and the setting right of their state. "That" is the subject, and what follows is the predicate, meaning: it occurs because of these people's following falsehood and those people's following truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that "that" is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimated form is "the matter is that," meaning: as has been mentioned, for this reason, so that the prepositional phrase and its object would be in the accusative position. End of quotation. There is no need for the omission given that this reading is sound without omission. "Falsehood" (al-batil) is what brings no benefit. Mujahid said: falsehood is Satan and everything that commands it, and truth is the Messenger and the Law (shar'). This kind of statement is what the scholars of rhetoric (bayan) call tafsir (explanation).

﴿Thus Allah sets forth﴾: Ibn Atiyya said: the reference is to the followers of the two groups mentioned, meaning: just as they followed these two paths, so the affair of each group is made clear, and a description of it is given through its kind of speech. The striking of a parable is from "striking" in the sense of "kind." Al-Zamakhshari said: "thus" means "like that manner of striking."

﴿Allah sets forth parables for people﴾: for the sake of people, so that they may take heed from them. If you ask: where is the striking of parables? I say: it lies in making the following of falsehood a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, and the following of truth a parable for the deeds of the believers; or in making the misguiding a parable for the failure of the disbelievers, and the remission of misdeeds a parable for the success of the believers.

﴿So when you encounter those who disbelieve﴾: that is, at whatever time you meet them, then kill them. In His words ﴿and kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], that is, in whatever place, so it is general in time and in place. Al-Zamakhshari said: "encounter" (laqītum) is from "liqā'," which means battle. End of quotation.

﴿Then striking of the necks﴾: this is a verbal noun (maṣdar) standing in place of the imperative verb, which is a common usage, and it is governed by an omitted verb. Scholars differ regarding its governing when what follows it is in the accusative. It was said: it is in the accusative by the verb that governs the verbal noun. It was also said: it is in the accusative by the verbal noun itself, since it stands in for its governing verb. An example of this is "darban Zaydan" (a striking of Zayd). The poet said:

*In a time when most of their concerns diverted people,*
*Then, O Zurayq of wealth, [snatch] like the snatching of foxes.*

This is the correct view, and His words "striking of the necks" show it, since it is the genitive construction of the verbal noun with its object. Had it not been operating as a governing element, its annexation to what follows would not be permitted. "Striking the necks" is an expression for killing. Since killing a person most often happens by striking his neck, this expression is used for killing; the particular necks are not intended, for during battle it is hardly possible to strike only the necks, rather fighting can take place on any part of the body. It is said: "the commander struck so-and-so's neck," or "struck his neck, his head, and whatever his eyes fall upon," meaning he killed him; just as His words "for what your hands have earned" [al-Shura: 30] express all other actions, since most earning is attributed to the hands. Al-Zamakhshari said: in this expression there is a harshness and severity that the word "killing" lacks, because it depicts killing in its most hideous form, namely severing the neck and removing the head, which is the top and highest part of the body and the most prominent of its organs. He added to this in His words ﴿above the necks and strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. End of quotation. This also encourages the believers, showing that the disbelievers are so near them that they can seize them when they are commanded to strike their necks.

﴿Until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them﴾: that is, you have caused much killing among them. This is the limit for the striking. When the massacre has occurred and they have gained control over those who were not killed, and they have bound the captives tightly, then ﴿either [release them] as a favour﴾ without ransom, ﴿or ransom﴾ until ﴿the war lays down its burdens﴾: that is, its loads and its implements. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

*I prepared for war its burdens:*
*tall spears and male horses.*

Ibn Atiyya quoted this verse for 'Amr, and al-Zamakhshari quoted it for al-A'sha. It was said: "burdens" here means sins, because in war there must be sins on one side or the other, and this is the limit. Mujahid said: [it lasts] until Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) descends. Qatada said: until everyone embraces Islam. It was also said: until you kill them. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent sense of the wording is a metaphor, meaning the commitment to the command forever, since the war between believers and disbelievers does not end its burdens, so this phrase came, just as you say: "I will do such-and-such until the Day of Resurrection," meaning you will do it constantly. Al-Zamakhshari said: the implements of war, meaning weapons and horses, are called "its burdens," because since there is no escape from carrying them, it is as though they are carried and borne alone; when [the war] ends, it is as though they are laid down. It was also said: "its burdens" means its sins, meaning until the people of war, the polytheists, abandon their polytheism and their disobedience by embracing Islam.

The apparent meaning is that striking the necks, which is killing, is limited by tightening the bonds at the time the massacre takes place, and that His words ﴿then either [release them] as a favour afterwards﴾, meaning after the binding, ﴿or ransom﴾, are two states for the captive: either he is freed as a favour, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, or he is ransomed, as it is reported from him (peace be upon him) that he ransomed two men from the disbelievers in exchange for one Muslim man.

The apparent meaning of this verse conflicts with His words: ﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid held that it has been abrogated (mansukha) by His words ﴿kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 5] and so on, and that taking captives, releasing them as a favour, and ransoming are lifted; so if a captive falls into the hands of the Muslims, he must be killed unless he embraces Islam. A similar view is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn Umar, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Ata', and al-Hasan held that this verse specifies the general wording of that one, and that the favour and ransom remain valid. Al-Hasan said: a captive is only killed in battle, to instil awe in the enemy by this. Most scholars held that the People of the Book may be released as a favour or ransomed, while idol-worshippers are only to be killed; so they specified the People of the Book from among the polytheists, and idol-worshippers were specified from among the disbelievers.

As for the position of the imams today: the position of Abu Hanifa is that the Imam has the choice between killing and enslaving; the position of al-Shafi'i is that he has the choice between killing, enslaving, ransoming, and releasing as a favour; and the position of Malik is that he has the choice between one of these four, and also the imposing of the jizya (the poll tax on non-Muslim subjects). The apparent meaning of His words ﴿or ransom﴾ permits ransoming him with wealth or with a Muslim captive. Al-Hasan said: he may not be ransomed with wealth.

As-Sulami recited ﴿fa-shiddū﴾ with a kasra on the shin (shīn); the majority recite it with a damma. "Al-wathāq" (the bonds) is with a fatha on the waw, and there is a dialect in which it is "al-wiqāq," which is the name for that with which one is bound. The words "mannan" and "fidā'an" are in the accusative by an omitted verb whose root must be estimated from their own wording, meaning: "either you bestow a favour, bestowing favour, or you ransom, ransoming." This verb must be omitted, because the verbal noun came as the detailing of an outcome, so its governing element is of the kind that must be omitted. A similar example is the poet's saying:

*I will certainly strive; either warding off a dreaded calamity,*
*or attaining the desired goal and hope.*

That is: "either I shall ward off the warding off of a dreaded calamity, or I shall attain the attaining of the desired goal." Abu al-Baqa' said: they may also be two objects (maf'ulayn), meaning: pay them as a favour, and accept; this is not a grammatical analysis (i'rab nahwi). Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, recited "wa-immā fidan" with a short vowel (qaṣr). Abu Hatim said: it is not permitted to shorten it, since it is the verbal noun of "fādaytuhu" (I ransomed him). This is not correct, for al-Farra' related four dialects for it: "fidā'an laka" with the long vowel and the imperative sense, "fidan laka" with a kasra, a ya' and tanwin, "fida laka" with shortening, and "fidā'un laka."

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿either as a favour﴾ is release without ransom, as the Messenger (peace be upon him) released Thumamah, and Abu Urwah al-Hajabi. In al-Zamakhshari's book it reads: "as he released Abu Urwah al-Hajabi and Uthal al-Hanafi," changing the kunya and the name; perhaps this was from the copyist, not in the original composition. It was also said: "mann" may mean: he bestows favour upon them by leaving off killing and having them enslaved, or he bestows favour upon them by letting them go in exchange for their accepting the jizya and becoming dhimmis (protected non-Muslim subjects).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 47, verse 1–11 (part 3 of 3):

It is apparent that His saying: ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for His saying: ﴿then bind them firmly﴾, because the striking of necks has already been made conditional on binding them firmly at the time of overpowering (al-ithkhan). It is not possible for it to be made conditional by another limit, since the two limits would conflict, unless the second is explanatory of the first and emphasizing it. Then it is permissible, because the binding of captives happens only until the war lays down its burdens. This applies when we interpret it as the disappearance of the strength of the unbelievers who are engaged at that time, and "the war" here means that which occurs at the time the believers meet the unbelievers. It is also permissible that the limited element be omitted and understood from the meaning, the estimate being: the ruling is that until the war lays down its burdens, meaning that no strength remains for them. Or, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, it is a metaphor meaning "until the Day of Resurrection," i.e., do that always. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what is 'until' attached?" I say: it must be attached either to the striking and binding, or to the granting of favour and ransom. The meaning according to both attachments, in the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, is that they continue in this state forever until there is a war with the polytheists, and that is when they have no strength left. It was also said: when Jesus son of Mary descends. And according to Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, it is attached to striking and binding. The meaning is: they are killed and taken captive until the kind of war lays down its burdens, and that is until the polytheists have no strength left. If it is attached to granting favour and ransom, the meaning is: they are granted favour and ransomed until the war of Badr lays down its burdens, until the granting of favour and ransom is taken, meaning: by setting them free from killing and enslaving them, that is, by allowing them to remain under the imposition of the jizyah by being among the People of the Covenant (dhimmah), and by the punishment that they be ransomed in exchange for the captives of the polytheists among the captives of the Muslims. Al-Tahawi narrated this as the school of Abu Hanifah, but the well-known view is that he does not permit their ransom with wealth or otherwise, out of fear that they would return as enemies to the Muslims. (That) i.e., the matter is that, if they do it.

﴿That, and had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them﴾: i.e., He would have punished them with some of the causes of destruction, such as a sinking into the earth, or a quake, or a violent wind, or drowning, or a overwhelming death.

﴿But that He may test﴾: i.e., but He commanded you to fight so that He may test some of you, namely the believers, by means of others, namely the unbelievers, by having them strive and endure, and having the unbelievers be hastened at their hands with some of the punishment due to them. Al-Jumhur read qatalu (qaatalu), with a fatha on the qaf and ta, without an alif; Qatadah, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read qutilu, in the passive, with a light ta; Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Isa and al-Jahdari likewise. 'Ali read: fa-lan yudalla, in the passive, their deeds being the subject, in the nominative. It was also read: yadilla, with a fatha on the ya, from dalla, their deeds being in the nominative.

﴿He will guide them﴾: i.e., to the path of Paradise. Mujahid said: the people of Paradise will find their way to their dwellings in it without error, for they were its inhabitants since they were created, and they will not be confused about it. 'Iyad narrated from Abu 'Amr: wa-yudkhilhumu (and He will admit them). And "yawma yajma'kum li-yawm al-jam'" and "innama nut'imukum" with the consonant of the word's lam pronounced with sukun.

﴿He made it known to them﴾: From Muqatil: the angel who was assigned to guard his deeds in this world walks before him and informs him of everything God has given him. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid and Qatadah said: its meaning is that He made them recognize it, i.e., made them know their abodes in it. In a hadith: "One of you is more knowledgeable of his abode in Paradise than of his abode in this world." It was also said: He named it for them and marked each dwelling with its owner, and this is a kind of making known. It is said: "He knew the house and marked its boundaries," i.e., he delimited it, so each person's paradise is set apart from others. And al-'Urf and al-Urf mean boundaries. It was also said: He honored it for them, raised it and elevated it, and this is from the a'raf, which are the mountains and what resembles them. Mawrij and others said: He made it fragrant, derived from al-'arf, and from it: "a food that is 'arrafa," i.e., made fragrant, as one says "'arrafa al-qidr," meaning he made the pot fragrant with salt and seasoning.

﴿If you help God﴾: i.e., His religion; (He will help you): i.e., against your enemies, by creating strength in you and other such means of knowledge.

﴿And make your feet firm﴾: i.e., in the places of war, or upon the path of Islam. Al-Jumhur read wa-yuthabbit (with shaddah), and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read it without shaddah.

﴿Then, destruction for them﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a distance (from good) for them; Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi: grief for them; al-Hasan: cursing; Ibn Zayd: wretchedness; al-Dahhak: humiliation; and al-Naqqash related: ugliness. (And those who disbelieved): is a subject (mubtada'), and the fa' enters into the predicate of the subject, its estimate being: fa-ta'isahumu Allah ta'san (so God causes them to stumble with a stumbling). So ta'san is in the accusative by a hidden verb, and for this reason the verb "and He made their deeds go astray" is conjoined to it. It is also permissible that alladhina be in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by His saying "then, destruction for them," as you say "Zaydan, jad'an lahu." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "On what is His saying 'and He made their deeds go astray' conjoined?" I say: on the verb that governed ta'san, because the meaning is: "he said ta'san for them" or "he decreed ta'san for them," and ta'san lahum is the opposite of la'an lahu. End quote. And it is better to supply a verb from the same root as the verbal noun, because this indicates what was omitted. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means in this world killing, and in the Hereafter falling headlong into the Fire. End quote. In His saying "fa-ta'san lahum," i.e., destruction, with a particle that strengthens the hearts of the believers, since He gave them firmness, and gave the unbelievers destruction and stumbling.

﴿That is because they hated what God revealed﴾: it includes what was revealed of the Qur'an in clarifying monotheism, mentioning resurrection, the obligatory duties and limits, and other things the Qur'an contains. (So He made their deeds fruitless): i.e., He made them among the deeds which do not grow and are not counted.

﴿God destroyed them utterly﴾: i.e., He ruined for them what they were specially attached to of their own selves, their children and their wealth, and all that belonged to them and to the unbelievers like them. That is the outcome and the destruction indicated by "destroyed" and the ruin, because destruction indicates it; or the sunnah, by His saying, "the sunnah of God concerning those who passed before." The first interpretation is the preferred one, because the outcome is stated explicitly, so the pronoun refers back to what is spoken, and what follows is the content of the saying. (That is because): an inceptive and predicate, and the indication of "that" refers, in the choice of a group, to the victory, and to the destruction, as He said: ﴿and for the unbelievers there are similar ones﴾. He said that the destruction which was made for the unbelievers at the hands of the believers is because God is their protector (mawla), i.e., their helper and supporter, and because the unbelievers have no helper, since they took gods that neither benefit nor harm, and abandoned the worship of Him who benefits and harms, namely God, exalted is He.

Qatadah said: this verse was revealed on the day of Uhud, and from it the Messenger of God ﷺ took his reply to Abu Sufyan when he said: "Say: God is our Protector, and you have no protector," when the polytheists said: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 47, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 3)**

(Surat al-Qital, forty verses, Madani.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

(p-70) ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, He will absolve them of their misdeeds and set right their state.﴾ ﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, while those who believe follow the truth from their Lord. Thus Allah sets forth their parables for mankind.﴾ ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, bind them firmly. Then either grant them release or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens. That is the case. Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them Himself, but He tests some of you by means of others. As for those who are slain in the way of Allah, He will not let their deeds go astray.﴾ ﴿He will guide them and set right their state.﴾ ﴿And He will admit them to the Garden, which He has made known to them.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you and make your feet firm.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is ruin, and He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah has sent down, so He has nullified their deeds.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? Allah destroyed them, and there await the disbelievers similar things.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾

(This surah is Madani according to the majority. Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said it is Makki. Ibn Atiyyah said it is Madani by consensus, but that is not as he said. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that it is Madani except for one verse, which was revealed after his Hajj, when he left Makkah and began looking towards the House. That verse is: "And how many a town..." The connection between its beginning and the end of what precedes it is very clear.)

**Linguistic notes**

*al-bal* (the mind, the thought): it means *al-fikr* (reflection). One says, "such-and-such occurred to my mind" (*kadha*). It is not made dual or plural, though the irregular plural *balat* has been reported.

*ta'asa* (to stumble and fall): *ta'isa* with a fatha on the ʿayn, *ta'san*, is the opposite of *tanaʿʿush* (to be raised up), and Allah makes one *ta'isa*. Mujammi' ibn Hilal said:

*"She says, having separated me from her husband: 'You have stumbled, as you made me stumble, O Mujammiʿ.'"*

Some, among them Amr ibn Shumayl and Abu al-Haytham, said *ta'iba* with a kasra on the ʿayn. From Abu Ubaydah: *ta'isahu Allah* and *at'asahu Allah* belong to the pattern *fa'ila* and *af'ala*. Ibn as-Sikkit said: *at-ta's* is to be dragged upon the face, and *an-naks* is to be dragged upon the head. He also said, and Tha'lab with him, that *at-ta's* is destruction. Al-Aʿsha said:

*"With a she-camel that is pale-hued, sturdy, and swift, when she stumbles, then 'ruin' is more fitting for her than my saying 'ʿaʿa'."*

*asin* (stagnant, foul-smelling water): water whose smell has changed. The verb is *yaʾsinu* and *yaʾsunu*. Tha'lab mentioned it in *al-Fasih*. The verbal noun is *usun* and *asin* with a kasra on the sin. *Yaʾsanu* with a fatha is a dialect form, reported by al-Yazidi. *Asina ar-rajul*, with a kasra only, means that a man entered a well, was struck by a smell from the well, and fainted or became dizzy. The poet said:

*"I shall leave the opponent pale, his fingertips yellowed, swaying in the wind like one who has been overcome by the well's stench."*

*ashrat* (signs, indications): the singular is *shart*, with a sukun or a fatha on the raʾ. Abu al-Aswad said:

*"If you have resolved to sever our bond, then the signs of its beginning have already appeared."*

*Ashrata ar-rajul nafsahu* means he obliged himself to certain duties. Aws ibn Hajar said:

*"So he bound himself to them, while he was a man of firm grip, and he cast himself upon his means and relied on them."*

*al-ʿasal* (honey) is well known. ʿAsal ibn Dhakwan was an early grammarian. *al-miʿa* (intestines): it is a maqsur noun whose alif is converted from a ya', as shown by its dual *miʿayan*, with the alif changed to ya'. *Al-miʿa* is what is in the belly of the intestines.

*al-qufl* (lock) is well known, and its root meaning is dryness and hardness. *Al-qufl* and *al-qafil* are wood that has dried up. *Al-qafil* is also a plant, and it is also a whip. *Aqfalahu as-sawm* means fasting dried him out. Al-Jawhari said this.

*ayifan* and *a'nifan* (just now): both are active participles, and their verb is not used. The verb that is used is *i'tanafa*. Both mean "beginning" (*mubtadiʾan*). Interpreting them as "the Hour" is an interpretation of meaning. Az-Zajjaj said: it derives from *istanaftu ash-shayʾ*, meaning I began the thing.

*fa-awla lahum*: the author of *as-Sihah* said: the Arabs' saying *awla laka* is a threat and warning, and from it is the poet's line:

*"Awla, then awla, then awla, and is there for the house any return from its milk?"*

End of his words. They differed over whether *awla* is a noun or a verb. Al-Asmaʿi held that it means that which destruction approaches, i.e., it came near to him. He recited:

*"They became hostile between the two front-ones, and it was near that it would exceed three."*

That is, it came near to exceeding. Tha'lab said: no one has said anything better about *awla* than what al-Asmaʿi said. Al-Mubarrad said: it is said to one who is about to perish. It is reported that a Bedouin would constantly shoot at game, which would escape from him, so he would say, "Awla laka (woe to you), you shot at game." He came near to hitting it, then it escaped from him. He said:

*"Had awla fed the people their game, but awla leaves the people hungry."*

Most scholars hold that it is a noun. It is said to be derived from *al-wali*, which is nearness, as the poet said:

*"Layla burdens me, though her nearness has gone far, and the vicissitudes have returned between us."*

Al-Jurjani said: it is what has been transformed from *al-waylu* (woe), so it is *afʿal* from it, but there is inversion in it.

*ad-dighn* and *ad-daghina* (rancour, grudge): the hatred. ʿAmr ibn Kulthum said:

*"Rancour after rancour spreads against you, and the hidden disease comes out."*

One says *daghina* with a kasra, and *tadaghana al-qawm* and *adghanu* mean they harboured grudges. *Daghina ʿalayhi* means he bore a grudge against him. *Adghanta as-sabiyya* means you took the child under your arm. Al-Ahmar recited:

*"As if he were a rancorous one who hides a child."*

Ibn Muqbil said:

*"And I did not rancorously hide my weapon at its battle."*

*Faras daghin* is a horse that does not give what it has of running except under beating. The root of the word is from *ad-dighn*, which is twisting and bending in the legs of an animal, a spear, and everything. Bishr said:

*"Like the one with bent legs walking in the alley."*

Al-Layth recited:

*"Indeed my young girl, from the spears' well-knotted (ones), the straightening did not increase her except rancour."*

Hatred in the heart is likened to it. Qutrub said:

*"And al-Layth made hostility more hidden."*

The poet said:

*"Say to the son of Hind: I did not intend by my speech anything except that friendship has grown and hostility has been built up."*

*laḥantu lahu*, with a fatha on the ḥa': *alḥanu laḥnan*. I said to him a statement which he understands from you and which is hidden from others. *Laḥina-hu* with a kasra means he understood it. *Alḥanahu* means he made him understand. *Alḥantuhu anā iyyāhu* and *lāḥantu an-nās* mean I outwitted people. The poet said:

*"Speech that is correct and that subtly alludes, and the best speech is that which is allusive."*

Al-Qattal al-Kilabi said:

*"And indeed I spoke to you so that you would understand, and I alluded in an allusion that is not doubtful."*

It is said that *laḥn al-qawl* means departing from what is correct, and it is taken from *al-laḥn* in grammar (i.e., error in inflection). *Wataraha* means he diminished it, taken from *adh-dhahl* (enmity). It is said it is taken from *al-watr*, which is singular.

(p-72) ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar others from the way of Allah, He has rendered their deeds void.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds, and believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, He has absolved them of their misdeeds and set right their state.﴾ ﴿That is because those who disbelieve follow falsehood, while those who believe follow the truth from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Thus Allah sets forth their parables for mankind.﴾ ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, bind them firmly. Then either grant them release or take ransom, until the war lays down its burdens.﴾ ﴿That is the case. Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them Himself, but He tests some of you by means of others. As for those who are slain in the way of Allah, He will not let their deeds go astray.﴾ ﴿He will guide them and set right their state.﴾ ﴿And He will admit them to the Garden, which He has made known to them.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, if you help Allah, He will help you and make your feet firm.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is ruin, and He will render their deeds void.﴾ ﴿That is because they disliked what Allah has sent down, so He has nullified their deeds.﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ ﴿Allah destroyed them, and there await the disbelievers similar things.﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾

This surah is Madani according to the majority. Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr and as-Suddi said it is Makki. Ibn Atiyyah said it is Madani by consensus, but that is not as he said. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that it is Madani except for one verse, which was revealed after his Hajj, when he left Makkah and began looking towards the House. That verse is: "And how many a town..." The connection between its beginning and the end of what precedes it is very clear.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 47, verses 1–11 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾: that is, they turned away from entering Islam, or they barred others from it. They are the people of Makkah who expelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas said: they are the ones who gave food [to the Quraysh] on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: they were twelve men from among the polytheists, who barred people from Islam and commanded them to disbelieve. It was also said: they are the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), who barred those among them and others who wished to enter Islam. Al-Dahhak said: "the way of Allah" means the House of Allah, preventing those who seek it, and it is general to everyone who disbelieves and bars [others].

﴿He has made their deeds go astray﴾: that is, He has destroyed them, since no good or benefit came from them, but only pure harm. It was also said: this verse was revealed at Badr, and that the reference in His words "He has made their deeds go astray" is to the agreement they made during their journey to Badr. It was also said: the intended "deeds" are their good acts in the pre-Islamic period (jahiliyya), such as maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, and the like, and the wording covers all of that.

﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: they are the Ansar (the Helpers of Madinah). Muqatil said: they are some people from Quraysh. It was also said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. It was also said: the verse is general, and even if the cause of revelation is specific to the two groups, the wording encompasses every disbeliever and every believer.

﴿And believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾: singling him out from among what must be believed in is an exalting of the Messenger's station and an informing that faith is neither valid nor complete except through him. This is emphasised by the parenthetical clause, which is: ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾. It was said: "and it is the truth" abrogates what came before it, and abrogation (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) does not apply to it. The majority of readers recite "nuzzila" in the passive voice; Zayd ibn Ali and Ibn Miqsam recite "nazzala" in the active voice; al-A'mash recites "unzila," with the hamza making it transitive, in the passive voice. It was also read as "nazala," in the triliteral form.

﴿He will remit their misdeeds and set right their state﴾: that is, their condition (ḥāl), said Qatada; their affairs (sha'n), said Mujahid; their matter (amr), said Ibn Abbas. The literal meaning of the word "bal" (state of mind, concern) is "thought," and the place where a person's attention lies is the heart. When that is made right, his condition is made right, so the wording points to the soundness of their creed, and the rest of their condition follows from it.

﴿That﴾: a reference to what was done to the disbelievers, namely the misguiding of their deeds, and to the believers, namely the remission of their misdeeds and the setting right of their state. "That" is the subject, and what follows is the predicate, meaning: it occurs because of these people's following falsehood and those people's following truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that "that" is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimated form is "the matter is that," meaning: as has been mentioned, for this reason, so that the prepositional phrase and its object would be in the accusative position. End of quotation. There is no need for the omission given that this reading is sound without omission. "Falsehood" (al-batil) is what brings no benefit. Mujahid said: falsehood is Satan and everything that commands it, and truth is the Messenger and the Law (shar'). This kind of statement is what the scholars of rhetoric (bayan) call tafsir (explanation).

﴿Thus Allah sets forth﴾: Ibn Atiyya said: the reference is to the followers of the two groups mentioned, meaning: just as they followed these two paths, so the affair of each group is made clear, and a description of it is given through its kind of speech. The striking of a parable is from "striking" in the sense of "kind." Al-Zamakhshari said: "thus" means "like that manner of striking."

﴿Allah sets forth parables for people﴾: for the sake of people, so that they may take heed from them. If you ask: where is the striking of parables? I say: it lies in making the following of falsehood a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, and the following of truth a parable for the deeds of the believers; or in making the misguiding a parable for the failure of the disbelievers, and the remission of misdeeds a parable for the success of the believers.

﴿So when you encounter those who disbelieve﴾: that is, at whatever time you meet them, then kill them. In His words ﴿and kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], that is, in whatever place, so it is general in time and in place. Al-Zamakhshari said: "encounter" (laqītum) is from "liqā'," which means battle. End of quotation.

﴿Then striking of the necks﴾: this is a verbal noun (maṣdar) standing in place of the imperative verb, which is a common usage, and it is governed by an omitted verb. Scholars differ regarding its governing when what follows it is in the accusative. It was said: it is in the accusative by the verb that governs the verbal noun. It was also said: it is in the accusative by the verbal noun itself, since it stands in for its governing verb. An example of this is "darban Zaydan" (a striking of Zayd). The poet said:

*In a time when most of their concerns diverted people,*
*Then, O Zurayq of wealth, [snatch] like the snatching of foxes.*

This is the correct view, and His words "striking of the necks" show it, since it is the genitive construction of the verbal noun with its object. Had it not been operating as a governing element, its annexation to what follows would not be permitted. "Striking the necks" is an expression for killing. Since killing a person most often happens by striking his neck, this expression is used for killing; the particular necks are not intended, for during battle it is hardly possible to strike only the necks, rather fighting can take place on any part of the body. It is said: "the commander struck so-and-so's neck," or "struck his neck, his head, and whatever his eyes fall upon," meaning he killed him; just as His words "for what your hands have earned" [al-Shura: 30] express all other actions, since most earning is attributed to the hands. Al-Zamakhshari said: in this expression there is a harshness and severity that the word "killing" lacks, because it depicts killing in its most hideous form, namely severing the neck and removing the head, which is the top and highest part of the body and the most prominent of its organs. He added to this in His words ﴿above the necks and strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. End of quotation. This also encourages the believers, showing that the disbelievers are so near them that they can seize them when they are commanded to strike their necks.

﴿Until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them﴾: that is, you have caused much killing among them. This is the limit for the striking. When the massacre has occurred and they have gained control over those who were not killed, and they have bound the captives tightly, then ﴿either [release them] as a favour﴾ without ransom, ﴿or ransom﴾ until ﴿the war lays down its burdens﴾: that is, its loads and its implements. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

*I prepared for war its burdens:*
*tall spears and male horses.*

Ibn Atiyya quoted this verse for 'Amr, and al-Zamakhshari quoted it for al-A'sha. It was said: "burdens" here means sins, because in war there must be sins on one side or the other, and this is the limit. Mujahid said: [it lasts] until Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) descends. Qatada said: until everyone embraces Islam. It was also said: until you kill them. Ibn Atiyya said: the apparent sense of the wording is a metaphor, meaning the commitment to the command forever, since the war between believers and disbelievers does not end its burdens, so this phrase came, just as you say: "I will do such-and-such until the Day of Resurrection," meaning you will do it constantly. Al-Zamakhshari said: the implements of war, meaning weapons and horses, are called "its burdens," because since there is no escape from carrying them, it is as though they are carried and borne alone; when [the war] ends, it is as though they are laid down. It was also said: "its burdens" means its sins, meaning until the people of war, the polytheists, abandon their polytheism and their disobedience by embracing Islam.

The apparent meaning is that striking the necks, which is killing, is limited by tightening the bonds at the time the massacre takes place, and that His words ﴿then either [release them] as a favour afterwards﴾, meaning after the binding, ﴿or ransom﴾, are two states for the captive: either he is freed as a favour, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) freed Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, or he is ransomed, as it is reported from him (peace be upon him) that he ransomed two men from the disbelievers in exchange for one Muslim man.

The apparent meaning of this verse conflicts with His words: ﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid held that it has been abrogated (mansukha) by His words ﴿kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 5] and so on, and that taking captives, releasing them as a favour, and ransoming are lifted; so if a captive falls into the hands of the Muslims, he must be killed unless he embraces Islam. A similar view is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn Umar, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Ata', and al-Hasan held that this verse specifies the general wording of that one, and that the favour and ransom remain valid. Al-Hasan said: a captive is only killed in battle, to instil awe in the enemy by this. Most scholars held that the People of the Book may be released as a favour or ransomed, while idol-worshippers are only to be killed; so they specified the People of the Book from among the polytheists, and idol-worshippers were specified from among the disbelievers.

As for the position of the imams today: the position of Abu Hanifa is that the Imam has the choice between killing and enslaving; the position of al-Shafi'i is that he has the choice between killing, enslaving, ransoming, and releasing as a favour; and the position of Malik is that he has the choice between one of these four, and also the imposing of the jizya (the poll tax on non-Muslim subjects). The apparent meaning of His words ﴿or ransom﴾ permits ransoming him with wealth or with a Muslim captive. Al-Hasan said: he may not be ransomed with wealth.

As-Sulami recited ﴿fa-shiddū﴾ with a kasra on the shin (shīn); the majority recite it with a damma. "Al-wathāq" (the bonds) is with a fatha on the waw, and there is a dialect in which it is "al-wiqāq," which is the name for that with which one is bound. The words "mannan" and "fidā'an" are in the accusative by an omitted verb whose root must be estimated from their own wording, meaning: "either you bestow a favour, bestowing favour, or you ransom, ransoming." This verb must be omitted, because the verbal noun came as the detailing of an outcome, so its governing element is of the kind that must be omitted. A similar example is the poet's saying:

*I will certainly strive; either warding off a dreaded calamity,*
*or attaining the desired goal and hope.*

That is: "either I shall ward off the warding off of a dreaded calamity, or I shall attain the attaining of the desired goal." Abu al-Baqa' said: they may also be two objects (maf'ulayn), meaning: pay them as a favour, and accept; this is not a grammatical analysis (i'rab nahwi). Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, recited "wa-immā fidan" with a short vowel (qaṣr). Abu Hatim said: it is not permitted to shorten it, since it is the verbal noun of "fādaytuhu" (I ransomed him). This is not correct, for al-Farra' related four dialects for it: "fidā'an laka" with the long vowel and the imperative sense, "fidan laka" with a kasra, a ya' and tanwin, "fida laka" with shortening, and "fidā'un laka."

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿either as a favour﴾ is release without ransom, as the Messenger (peace be upon him) released Thumamah, and Abu Urwah al-Hajabi. In al-Zamakhshari's book it reads: "as he released Abu Urwah al-Hajabi and Uthal al-Hanafi," changing the kunya and the name; perhaps this was from the copyist, not in the original composition. It was also said: "mann" may mean: he bestows favour upon them by leaving off killing and having them enslaved, or he bestows favour upon them by letting them go in exchange for their accepting the jizya and becoming dhimmis (protected non-Muslim subjects).
