I say: its being bare of the particle of denial contains an increase in depicting the obstinacy of one who equates between the one who holds fast to the clear proof and the one who follows his desire, and that he is like one who affirms equality between the Garden, in which those rivers flow, and the Fire, whose inhabitants are given boiling water to drink. A parallel to this is the saying of a poet:

"I rejoice that I am bereaved of the noble, and that I inherit a few camels, short-tailed, dark in color."

This is a statement denying the joy at the loss of the noble and at inheriting camels, despite its being bare of the particle of denial, because it falls under the ruling of one who says: "Do you rejoice at the death of your brother and at inheriting his camels?" The purpose for which the particle of denial was dropped is to depict the ugliness of what he has been afflicted with. It is as if he said: "Yes, someone like me rejoices at the loss of the noble, and at replacing them with a few camels whose value is small," and this is from the kind of submission under which every denial lies. End of quote. From this it is concluded that there is agreement on the parsing of (mathalu al-jannah) as a subject, and they differ over the predicate: it is said that it is mentioned, namely (kaman huwa khālidun fi al-nār); it is said that it is omitted, and it is said that it is supposed to come before it, which is the view of Sibawayh, or after it, which is the view of al-Naḍr and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah according to the difference in estimation. When he (God) clarified the difference between the two groups in guidance and misguidance, He clarified the difference between them in their final outcome. Just as He put first the one who is upon a clear proof before the one who follows his desire, He put first their condition before the other's condition.

Ibn Kathīr and the people of Makkah read: (āsin, "unchanging") in the pattern of fāʿil, from (asana), with a fatḥah on the sīn. It is also read: (ghayri yāsin) with a yāʾ. Abū ʿAlī said: That is by lightening the hamzah.

﴿لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ﴾, and others. (ladhdhatin): the feminine form of (ladhdh), meaning delicious, and it is a verbal noun used as an adjective. The majority read it in the genitive (jarr) as an attribute of (khamr, "wine"). It is also read in the nominative (raf') as an attribute of (anhār, "rivers"), and in the accusative (naṣb), meaning for the sake of delight, in which case it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

﴿مِن عَسَلٍ مُصَفًّى﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: It has not come out of the bellies of bees. It was said: so that it would be mixed with wax and other things. He described it as purified (muṣaffā) because the predominant gender for honey is masculine, and it is one of those words that can be masculine or feminine. It is related from Kaʿb that the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Jayḥān are among these rivers in the Garden. There is disagreement regarding identifying each one, namely from which of them they descend. The rivers are arranged beginning with water, which is what cannot be done without among drinks; then milk, since it takes the place of foods among many of the staple foods of the Arabs and others; then wine, because when quenching of thirst and food are achieved, the soul yearns for what it delights in; then honey, because in it is healing in this world from what afflicts drink and food, so it is later in its arrangement.

﴿ولَهم فِيها مِن كُلِّ الثَّمَراتِ﴾: It was also said that the subject is omitted, meaning: kinds of every fruit. Some of them estimated it with His saying (zawjān, "two kinds"). (wa-maghfiratun min rabbihim, "and forgiveness from their Lord"): because forgiveness comes before entering the Garden, or it is by omission, meaning: with a blessing of forgiveness, since forgiveness is the cause of bliss.

﴿وسُقُوا﴾: refers to the meaning of man (man), and (khālidun) refers to its wording. Likewise (kharajū, "they went out"): in the sense of man (man) (yastamiʿu, "who listens"). The hypocrites used to attend the Messenger and listen to his speech and recitation, and when they went out, ﴿قالُوا لِلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا العِلْمَ﴾, namely those who truly listened to the Messenger's speech and retained it: ﴿ماذا قالَ آنِفًا﴾ "What did he just say?" meaning just now. This was in a manner of mockery and belittlement, meaning: we did not understand what he says, and we did not know what benefit there is in that. Among those they asked was Ibn Masʿūd. (āniful, "just now") is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), that is, it is a subject (mubtadaʾ), meaning: what is the statement that he began just before separating from him? The majority read (āniful) in the pattern of fāʿil, and Ibn Kathīr in the pattern of faʿil. Al-Zamakhsharī said: (āniful) is put in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). End of quote. He said that because he explained it as "just now." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, and the commentators say: (āniful) means the recent past hour close to us, and this is an explanation by meaning. End of quote. The correct view is that it is not an adverb of time, and we do not know of any grammarian who counted it among the adverbs of time.

The pronoun in (zādahum, "He increased them") refers to God, as shown by His statement (ṭabaʿa Allāhu, "God sealed"), since it is their counterpart, and as it is in (wa-ātāhum, "and gave them"). The increase in this sense is by increasing understanding and proofs, or by the revelation of the Law with commands, prohibitions and reports, so the guided one grows in knowledge of that and in faith in it. It was said: It is possible that it refers to the statement of the hypocrites and their confusion, because that is something at which the believer marvels, praises God for his faith, and increases in support of his religion. It was also said: it refers to the statement of the Messenger. (wa-ātāhum taqwāhum, "and gave them their piety"): meaning He gave them, that is, made them God-fearing toward Him, so their piety is a verbal noun (maṣdar) attached to the agent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 47, verse 12–19 (part 2 of 2):

(أنْ تَأْتِيَهم): a substitutive apposition (badal ishtimal) of "al-Sa'ah" (the Hour), and the pronoun refers to the hypocrites; that is, the matter that actually occurs is their awaiting the Hour, even though they themselves, in their own souls, are awaiting something other than that, because what is in their souls is not taken into account, for it is false. Abu Ja'far al-Rawwasi, on the authority of the people of Makkah, read: (an ta'tihim), in the conditional form, whose response is: ﴿فَقَدْ جاءَ أشْراطُها﴾ ("then its signs have indeed come"). This is not doubtful, because it is certainly coming. Rather, they were addressed in terms of the doubt they had been in, and its meaning is: if you doubt its establishment, then its signs (a'lamuha) have indeed come, so the doubt returns to the addressees who doubt. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "What is the response of the condition?" I say: their statement ﴿فَأنّى لَهُمْ﴾ ("then how will they have it"). Its meaning is: when the Hour comes upon them, how will they have their reminder (dhikraahum), that is, their remembrance and admonition? When the Hour comes upon them, meaning the reminder will not benefit them at that time, due to His saying: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَذَكَّرُ الإنْسانُ وأنّى لَهُ الذِّكْرى﴾ [al-Fajr: 23]. If you say: With what is His saying "and its signs have indeed come" connected, according to the two readings? I say: With the coming of the Hour, as the connection of cause to effect, like your saying: "If Zayd honors me, then I am worthy of honor; I honor him."

Al-Ja'fi and Harun, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read (baghtatan), with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the ta'. The author of al-Lawami' (Sahib al-Lawami') said: It is an adjective, and its accusative is in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal). It has no parallel among verbal nouns (masadir) or adjectives, but among nouns, such as al-hurriyyah (freedom), which is a collective noun, and al-sariyyah, which is a place name. End of quotation. Likewise said Abu al-'Abbas ibn al-Hajj, one of the companions of the master Abu 'Ali al-Shalawbini, in (Kitab al-Masadir) regarding Abu 'Amr: that the correct form should be baghtatan, with a fatha on the ghayn without shadda, like the reading of al-Hasan mentioned earlier. End of quotation. This is in keeping with his habit of disparaging transmissions.

﴿فَقَدْ جاءَ أشْراطُها﴾: that is, its signs (a'lamatuha), so one should prepare for it. Among the signs of the Hour is the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he is the Seal of the Prophets. It is related from him that he said: "I am among the signs of the Hour." And he said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and like the two horses of a race. It was said: among them are the smoke and the splitting of the moon. And from al-Kalbi: the abundance of wealth, and commerce, and false testimony, and the severing of kinship ties, and the scarcity of the noble, and the abundance of the base.

﴿فَأنّى لَهم إذا جاءَتْهم ذِكْراهُمْ﴾: The apparent meaning is: how will they have the reminder and acting upon it when the Hour comes upon them? That is, that has already passed them by. It was said: It is possible that the subject is omitted, meaning: then how will they have deliverance when the reminder comes to them with what they were told of, and they denied it, by its being followed by punishment? Then He turned away from mentioning the hypocrites and said: ﴿فاعْلَمْ أنَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا اللَّهُ﴾ ("so know that there is no god but Allah"), and the meaning is: persist in your action with monotheism. This was used as evidence against the view of those who say that the first of the obligations is knowledge and reflection before speech and affirmation. In the verse there is also what indicates humility and the abasement of the self, since He commanded him to seek forgiveness, and along with others, to seek forgiveness for them.

﴿مُتَقَلَّبَكُمْ﴾: your movement (mutasarrifakum) in your worldly life.

﴿ومَثْواكُمْ﴾: your dwelling in your graves and in your Hereafter. 'Ikrimah said: your movement in the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers, and your dwelling (mathwakum): your residence on the earth. al-Tabari and others said: your movement (mutaqallabakum): your activity in your wakefulness, and your dwelling (mathwakum): your sleep. It was said: your movement in your livelihoods and your trades, and your dwelling where you are driven out of your homes. It was said: mutaqallabakum with the letter ta', and Ibn 'Abbas with the letter nun.

(p. 81) The believers were eager for the triumph of Islam, the exaltation of its word, and the wish to kill the enemy. They found companionship in revelation and felt lonely when it was delayed. God, the Exalted, has made this a fixed gate and an established rule that may not be transgressed. So God praised the believers for their request that a sura be sent down, and the meaning includes Our command to fight the enemy and to expose the hypocrites. Apparently those who made this request were sincere in their faith, and for this reason He said afterwards, ﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They claimed eagerness for jihad and wished for it with their tongues, and they said, ﴿Why has a sura not been sent down?﴾ meaning concerning jihad.

﴿But when a sura is sent down﴾, and they were commanded in it to do what they had wished for and longed for, they recoiled, it was hard for them, and they were dismayed, like His saying: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. End of quotation. In this there is a warning contained in the wording of the Qur'an. And (lawla) means "why not" (hal-la). Abu Malik said: (la) is superfluous, and the construction is "if a sura were sent down," but this is nothing. It was read as "fa-idha nazalat" (when it descended). Zayd ibn Ali read "sura muhkama" with the accusative in both words, and the nominative of nuzzilat is pronounced with a damma, and "sura" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). He and Ibn Umar read "wa-dhukira" in the active voice, meaning God.

﴿Therein fighting is mentioned﴾. The majority read "sura muhkama" in the nominative, as the subject of a passive verb, and "dhukira" in the passive, with "al-qital" (fighting) as its substitute subject. Its being "muhkama" means that it is not abrogated. Qatada said: Every sura in which there is fighting is muhkama among the Qur'an, not specifically this verse, because fighting abrogated what had been truce and reconciliation, and it is not abrogated until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: muhkama means containing lawful and unlawful. It was also said: muhkama means that the literal meanings of its words are intended, as opposed to the mutashabih (ambiguous) in which a figurative sense is intended, such as His saying: ﴿The Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], ﴿in what I neglected concerning God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], ﴿so strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease, looking at you﴾: that is, their eyes stare from cowardice and terror.

﴿With the look of one fainting from death﴾: that is, a look like that of one who has been overcome by a faint because death has come upon him. It was also said: they do this, which is a fixed stare at the Messenger out of intense enmity. It was also said: out of fear of exposure, for if they hold back from fighting they will be disgraced and their hypocrisy will be made manifest. ﴿Woe to them﴾: its explanation has already been given in al-Mufradat (Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary). Qatada said: as if He said, "Punishment is more fitting for them." It was also said: they are the disliked. Its morphological pattern is afalu or aflu, according to the disagreement, because istif'al, which we mentioned in al-Mufradat [applies]. According to the view of the majority, it is a noun that is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "for them." It was also said: awla is the subject, "for them" is its complement, and "obedience" is the predicate; it is as if the lam has the sense of the ba': "so fitting for them is obedience." Al-Zamakhshari did not address its i'rab (grammatical analysis), but said: its meaning is a supplication against them, that what they dislike should befall them. According to al-Asma'i's view, it is a verb whose subject is an implied pronoun understood from the meaning; it is omitted because of frequency of use, as if he said: "it has approached them," that is, destruction. Ibn Atiyya said: The well-known usage of the Arabs is only "awla laka," alone, by way of ellipsis and abbreviation, because of the strength it carries; so one says, as a rebuke and threat: "Awla laka, O so-and-so." This verse is of this type. From it is His saying: "Awla laka fa-awla" (Woe to you, and then woe!). And the saying of al-Siddiq to al-Hasan, may God be pleased with them both: "Awla laka" (Woe to you!). End of quotation.

Most of them hold that ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾ is an independent sentence from which one of the two parts is omitted: either the predicate, whose implied form is "more fitting," which is the view of Mujahid and the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil; or the subject, whose implied form is "the matter is" or "we command obedience," that is, the matter pleasing to God is obedience. It was also said: it is a quotation of their words, that is, they said "obedience," and the reading of Ubayy supports this: "They say: obedience and fair speech." Their saying this was by way of mockery and deception. Qatada said: whoever stops at ﴿so woe to them, obedience﴾ begins a new sentence with the predicate, and the meaning is that this was from them by way of deception. It was also said: "obedience" is an attribute of "sura," meaning "so it is obedience," that is, something obeyed. This view is worthless because of the long separation between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿But when the matter is resolved﴾: that is, it becomes serious. ʿAzm means earnestness, and it belongs to the people of the matter. It is used metaphorically for the matter itself, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Surely that is among the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43]. The poet said:

*War has become earnest with them, so they became earnest.*

The apparent answer to "idha" (when) is His saying: ﴿then if they had been true to God﴾, just as you say: "When it is winter, then if you come to me I will clothe you." It was also said: the answer is omitted, and its implied form is: "when the matter is resolved, it is so-and-so, or the like," as Qatada said. Whoever takes "obedience and fair speech" to mean that they say it by way of deception estimates the omitted answer as "the matter is resolved, let them be taken to account and pressed." Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "then I would believe," so ﴿if they had been true to God﴾ in what they claimed of their eagerness for jihad, or in their faith, and their hearts had agreed with their tongues on it, or in their hearts, ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾.

﴿Then, would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ The phrase ﴿so would you perhaps﴾ is a shift (iltifat) toward those in whose hearts is a disease; He turned to them with direct address by way of rebuke and to make them confront the evil of their conduct. The disagreement over the usage of "asa" (perhaps) has already been discussed. Concerning its reading when a second-person pronoun is attached to it in the sura al-Baqara, the attachment of the pronoun to it is the usage of the Hijaz, while the Banu Tamim do not attach the pronoun to it. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: They have mentioned that "asa" takes attached pronouns of both the nominative and accusative, and that it does not take the pronoun ... And as for the saying of whoever said "asa anta taqum" (perhaps you stand) and "asa ana aqum" (perhaps I stand), it is beneath what has been mentioned, a lengthy point with what it contains. End of quotation. I know of no one among the transmitters of Arabic who mentioned the separate pronoun after "asa," and it is separated between "asa" and its predicate by the condition, which is ﴿if you turn away﴾.

The majority read ﴿if you turn away﴾, meaning if you turn away from Islam. Qatada said: How did you see the people when they turned away from the Book of God? Did they not shed forbidden blood, sever the ties of kinship, and disobey the Merciful? He refers to what happened during the interval (fatra) after the time of the Messenger. Ka'b, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: ﴿if you turn away﴾ means if you take charge of people's affairs through rule, and the reading "wulliitum" (passive) supports this. On this view it was said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayya. From the Prophet ﷺ: "in tawallaytum," with a damma on the ta' and the waw and a kasra on the lam, and with this reading ʿAli and Uways recited, meaning: if I put you in charge of an unjust rule, you will enter their worldly life, away from a just imam. And in the sense of "if you turn away" through punishment, exile, and the thwarting of the Arabs in their jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) and their practice of raids and their persistence in them, then if its fruit is corruption in the land and the severing of kinship. It was also said its meaning is: if the people take charge of you and God hands you over to them. The most evident view is that this is an address to the hypocrites concerning the matter of fighting, which is what the preceding verses were about, meaning: if you turn away from complying with God's command regarding fighting.

﴿That you cause corruption in the land﴾ by not helping the people of Islam; when you do not help them, you sever the ties of kinship between you and them. This is indicated by ﴿those whom God has cursed﴾. So all the verses are about the hypocrites. This expectation expressed by "asa" is not attributed to Him, the Exalted, because He knows what was and what will be; it is rather relative to those who know the hypocrites, as if He says to them: "We have knowledge from the vantage of their loss: Is it to be expected from you, if you turn away from fighting, that such and such will happen?" The majority read ﴿tuqatti'u﴾ with doubled tashdid for intensification; Abu Amr, in one narration, Sallam, Ya'qub, Aban and Isma: with a single tashdid, the imperfect of qata'a; al-Hasan read "wa-taqattaʿu," with a fatha on the ta' and the qaf, dropping the preposition, meaning "your kinships," because taqattaʿa is intransitive. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those in whose hearts is a disease; ﴿so He deafened them﴾ to hearing the admonition; ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ to the path of guidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: God cursed them for their corruption and their severing of kinship, so He withheld His kindnesses from them and forsook them until they were blinded. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). The construction came as ﴿fa-asammahum﴾ (so He deafened them) and did not come as "fa-asamma adhanahum" (deafened their ears); and it came as ﴿wa-a'mā abṣārahum﴾ (and blinded their eyes) and did not come as "wa-a'amahum" (blinded them). It was said: because if the ear were deafened it would not perceive sight; the eye has a role in seeing and the ear has a role in hearing. End of quotation. For this reason it came as ﴿and upon their hearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 7], and ﴿and made for you hearing﴾, and it did not come as "and upon their ears," nor "and made for you ears."

When the ear was mentioned, heaviness (waqr) was attributed to it, which is less than deafness, as He said: ﴿and in our ears is heaviness﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an?﴾: that is, do they not examine it and what it contains of admonitions, warnings, and threats against the disobedient? This is an interrogative of rebuke and confrontation directed at those who fight against it.

﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ This is a metaphor for those among them in whom there is faith. ʾAm (or) here is disjunctive, meaning "rather"; the hamza is interrogative for affirmation. It is not impossible for them that their hearts are locked, so that no reminder reaches them. The description of the hearts did not require definition, because it is known that they are the hearts of those mentioned. There is no need to estimate an omitted attribute, that is, "or upon hearts whose locks are hard." He attributed the locks to them, meaning the particular locks, or they are the locks of unbelief that were shut so that they cannot be opened. It was read "iqfaluha" with a kasra on the hamza, which is a verbal noun, and "aqfuluha" in the plural pattern af'ul.

﴿Indeed those who turned back upon their heels after guidance had become clear to them﴾. Qatada said: It was revealed concerning a group of Jews who knew the matter of the Messenger from the Torah, and guidance became clear to them in this way; but when they came into contact with his affair they envied him, and they turned back from that measure of guidance. Ibn Abbas and others said: It was revealed concerning hypocrites who had become Muslim, then their hearts died. The verse encompasses everyone who enters within the scope of its wording.

Earlier, the discussion of *sawwala* (سَوَّلَ) was given in the commentary on Surah Yusuf. al-Zamakhshari said: "*sawwala lahum* means he made the committing of great sins seem attractive to them. It derives from *al-sawl*, which means slackness, and whoever derives it from *al-su'l* (request) has no knowledge of morphology (*al-tasrif*) or derivation (*al-ishtiqaq*) at all." End of quote. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "It has the meaning of *wa-la hum min al-sawl*, which means slackness and dangling." Others said: *sawwalahum* means "he gave them false hope" (*rajjahum*). Ibn Bahr said: "He gave them what they asked for" (*aʿtahum suʾlahum*).

al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and he derived it from..." to the end of his words, is not sound, because he assumed that the root of *al-sul* is the hamza. The two roots are different: either the root of *sawwala* is *w* and the middle radical of *al-suʾl* is a hamza, or the word *al-sul* has two roots: one with hamza, from *sa'ala yas'alu* (to ask), and the other with waw, from *sala yasalu* (to flow). If that is so, *sawwala* may be from the hamza-root. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: "*Al-taswil* originally comes from relaxing (*al-irkha'*), and from it is the verse ﴿فَدَلّاهُما بِغُرُورٍ﴾ (So he lowered them by deception) [al-Araf: 22]. *Al-sawl* is the slackening of the belly."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿سَوَّلَ لَهُمْ﴾ as *kaydahu* (his scheme), with an omitted noun (*mudaf*) assumed.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وأمْلى لَهُمْ﴾ with the verb in the active voice (*mabniyyan lil-fa'il*). The apparent meaning is that the subject refers to Satan. This was also said by al-Hasan, who understood his false promise of survival as a form of granting life (*al-ibqaʾ*). *Al-ibqaʾ* is survival for a long period of time, with extended hopes and wishes given to them.

It was said that the subject of *amla* may be a pronoun referring to God, and this is the more preferred view, because the true meaning of *al-imla'* (granting respite) belongs to God.

Ibn Sirin, al-Jahdari, Shayba, Abu ʿAmr and ʿIsa read *wa-umliya* in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ul*), meaning they were given respite and their lives were extended.

Mujahid, Ibn Hurmuz, al-Aʿmash, Sallam and Yaʿqub read *wa-umli* with the first-person hamza (*hamzat al-mutakallim*), as the present tense of *amla*, meaning "and I give them respite," like God's words ﴿إنَّما نُمْلِي لَهُمْ﴾ (We only give them respite) [Al ʿImran: 178]. It may also be a past tense in which the *ya'* has been dropped, as you would say *yaʿi* with a silent *ya'*.

﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم قالُوا لِلَّذِينَ كَرِهُوا ما نَزَّلَ﴾ (That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down). It is narrated that a group from Qurayza and al-Nadir used to help the hypocrites in opposing the Messenger and in working against him by supporting and aiding them. This is the meaning of His words ﴿سَنُطِيعُكم في بَعْضِ الأمْرِ﴾ (We will obey you in some of the matter).

It was also said: the pronoun in *qalu* refers to the hypocrites, and "those who hated what God had sent down" are Qurayza and al-Nadir. "Some of the matter" is the hypocrites' statement to them: ﴿لَئِنْ أُخْرِجْتُمْ لَنَخْرُجَنَّ مَعَكُمْ﴾ (If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you) [al-Hashr: 11]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It was also said: "some of the matter" means denying the Messenger, or denying *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God), or abandoning fighting alongside him.

It was said: it is the statement of both groups, the Jews and the hypocrites, to the polytheists: "We will obey you in agreeing to be hostile to the Messenger and in staying away from struggle (*jihad*) alongside him." *Fi ba'd al-amr* is specified as "in some of what they conceal," or "in some of the matter that concerns you."

The majority of reciters read *asrarahum* with a hamza that has a fatha. Their secrets were many. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-Aʿmash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with a kasra on the hamza (*bi-kasriha*), which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). They said that this was said secretly among themselves, and God revealed it to them.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: "The more apparent reading is that God knows their secrets, which is what is in their hearts of knowledge of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). They were stubborn and arrogant, and they knew the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as they knew their own sons." End of quote.

﴿فَكَيْفَ إذا تَوَفَّتْهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (So how will it be when the angels take them at death?). The explanation of "those in whose hearts is a disease" has already been given, along with their reason for fighting. The statement of the apostates (*al-murtaddin*), and what awaits them of recompense for following the lies (*tawa'iyat al-kadhibin*) of what God has sent down, has also been given. And ﴿واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ إسْرارَهُمْ﴾ (and God knows their secrets) has been given. So this question, whose meaning is to make them aware (*al-tawqif*), comes after these things.

al-Tabari said: "So how is His knowledge of them, that is, of their secrets, when the angels take them at death?" It was also said: "So how will their condition be with God regarding what they committed of that statement?"

al-Aʿmash read *tawaffahum* with an alif in place of the taʾ. This may be either a past tense or a present tense with the taʾ omitted. The apparent meaning is that the time of death is the time of the taking of souls (*al-tawaffi*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "No one dies in a state of disobedience except that the angels strike his face and his back." The angels here are the Angel of Death and his assistants. It was also said: it is the time of fighting in support of the Messenger; they strike their faces so that they stand firm, and their backs so that they flee. *Al-malaʾika* here means "the help." The apparent meaning is that *yadribun* (striking) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-malaʾika*. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *tawaffahum*, but this is weak.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That): that is, that striking of faces and backs, ﴿بِأنَّهُمُ اتَّبَعُوا ما أسْخَطَ اللَّهَ﴾ (because they followed what angered God), which is disbelief, or concealing the sending of the Messenger, or Satan's enticement. These are several views. The one who follows something turns his face toward it, so it fits that the angels strike his face.

﴿وكَرِهُوا رِضْوانَهُ﴾ (and they disliked His pleasure): which is faith in God and following His religion. The disbeliever turns away from something, so it fits that the angels strike his back. In this there is a matching of two things with two things.

(p. 81) The believers were eager for the triumph of Islam, the exaltation of its word, and the wish to kill the enemy. They found companionship in revelation and felt lonely when it was delayed. God, the Exalted, has made this a fixed gate and an established rule that may not be transgressed. So God praised the believers for their request that a sura be sent down, and the meaning includes Our command to fight the enemy and to expose the hypocrites. Apparently those who made this request were sincere in their faith, and for this reason He said afterwards, ﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They claimed eagerness for jihad and wished for it with their tongues, and they said, ﴿Why has a sura not been sent down?﴾ meaning concerning jihad.

﴿But when a sura is sent down﴾, and they were commanded in it to do what they had wished for and longed for, they recoiled, it was hard for them, and they were dismayed, like His saying: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. End of quotation. In this there is a warning contained in the wording of the Qur'an. And (lawla) means "why not" (hal-la). Abu Malik said: (la) is superfluous, and the construction is "if a sura were sent down," but this is nothing. It was read as "fa-idha nazalat" (when it descended). Zayd ibn Ali read "sura muhkama" with the accusative in both words, and the nominative of nuzzilat is pronounced with a damma, and "sura" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). He and Ibn Umar read "wa-dhukira" in the active voice, meaning God.

﴿Therein fighting is mentioned﴾. The majority read "sura muhkama" in the nominative, as the subject of a passive verb, and "dhukira" in the passive, with "al-qital" (fighting) as its substitute subject. Its being "muhkama" means that it is not abrogated. Qatada said: Every sura in which there is fighting is muhkama among the Qur'an, not specifically this verse, because fighting abrogated what had been truce and reconciliation, and it is not abrogated until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: muhkama means containing lawful and unlawful. It was also said: muhkama means that the literal meanings of its words are intended, as opposed to the mutashabih (ambiguous) in which a figurative sense is intended, such as His saying: ﴿The Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], ﴿in what I neglected concerning God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], ﴿so strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease, looking at you﴾: that is, their eyes stare from cowardice and terror.

﴿With the look of one fainting from death﴾: that is, a look like that of one who has been overcome by a faint because death has come upon him. It was also said: they do this, which is a fixed stare at the Messenger out of intense enmity. It was also said: out of fear of exposure, for if they hold back from fighting they will be disgraced and their hypocrisy will be made manifest. ﴿Woe to them﴾: its explanation has already been given in al-Mufradat (Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary). Qatada said: as if He said, "Punishment is more fitting for them." It was also said: they are the disliked. Its morphological pattern is afalu or aflu, according to the disagreement, because istif'al, which we mentioned in al-Mufradat [applies]. According to the view of the majority, it is a noun that is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "for them." It was also said: awla is the subject, "for them" is its complement, and "obedience" is the predicate; it is as if the lam has the sense of the ba': "so fitting for them is obedience." Al-Zamakhshari did not address its i'rab (grammatical analysis), but said: its meaning is a supplication against them, that what they dislike should befall them. According to al-Asma'i's view, it is a verb whose subject is an implied pronoun understood from the meaning; it is omitted because of frequency of use, as if he said: "it has approached them," that is, destruction. Ibn Atiyya said: The well-known usage of the Arabs is only "awla laka," alone, by way of ellipsis and abbreviation, because of the strength it carries; so one says, as a rebuke and threat: "Awla laka, O so-and-so." This verse is of this type. From it is His saying: "Awla laka fa-awla" (Woe to you, and then woe!). And the saying of al-Siddiq to al-Hasan, may God be pleased with them both: "Awla laka" (Woe to you!). End of quotation.

Most of them hold that ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾ is an independent sentence from which one of the two parts is omitted: either the predicate, whose implied form is "more fitting," which is the view of Mujahid and the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil; or the subject, whose implied form is "the matter is" or "we command obedience," that is, the matter pleasing to God is obedience. It was also said: it is a quotation of their words, that is, they said "obedience," and the reading of Ubayy supports this: "They say: obedience and fair speech." Their saying this was by way of mockery and deception. Qatada said: whoever stops at ﴿so woe to them, obedience﴾ begins a new sentence with the predicate, and the meaning is that this was from them by way of deception. It was also said: "obedience" is an attribute of "sura," meaning "so it is obedience," that is, something obeyed. This view is worthless because of the long separation between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿But when the matter is resolved﴾: that is, it becomes serious. ʿAzm means earnestness, and it belongs to the people of the matter. It is used metaphorically for the matter itself, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Surely that is among the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43]. The poet said:

*War has become earnest with them, so they became earnest.*

The apparent answer to "idha" (when) is His saying: ﴿then if they had been true to God﴾, just as you say: "When it is winter, then if you come to me I will clothe you." It was also said: the answer is omitted, and its implied form is: "when the matter is resolved, it is so-and-so, or the like," as Qatada said. Whoever takes "obedience and fair speech" to mean that they say it by way of deception estimates the omitted answer as "the matter is resolved, let them be taken to account and pressed." Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "then I would believe," so ﴿if they had been true to God﴾ in what they claimed of their eagerness for jihad, or in their faith, and their hearts had agreed with their tongues on it, or in their hearts, ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾.

﴿Then, would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ The phrase ﴿so would you perhaps﴾ is a shift (iltifat) toward those in whose hearts is a disease; He turned to them with direct address by way of rebuke and to make them confront the evil of their conduct. The disagreement over the usage of "asa" (perhaps) has already been discussed. Concerning its reading when a second-person pronoun is attached to it in the sura al-Baqara, the attachment of the pronoun to it is the usage of the Hijaz, while the Banu Tamim do not attach the pronoun to it. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: They have mentioned that "asa" takes attached pronouns of both the nominative and accusative, and that it does not take the pronoun ... And as for the saying of whoever said "asa anta taqum" (perhaps you stand) and "asa ana aqum" (perhaps I stand), it is beneath what has been mentioned, a lengthy point with what it contains. End of quotation. I know of no one among the transmitters of Arabic who mentioned the separate pronoun after "asa," and it is separated between "asa" and its predicate by the condition, which is ﴿if you turn away﴾.

The majority read ﴿if you turn away﴾, meaning if you turn away from Islam. Qatada said: How did you see the people when they turned away from the Book of God? Did they not shed forbidden blood, sever the ties of kinship, and disobey the Merciful? He refers to what happened during the interval (fatra) after the time of the Messenger. Ka'b, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: ﴿if you turn away﴾ means if you take charge of people's affairs through rule, and the reading "wulliitum" (passive) supports this. On this view it was said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayya. From the Prophet ﷺ: "in tawallaytum," with a damma on the ta' and the waw and a kasra on the lam, and with this reading ʿAli and Uways recited, meaning: if I put you in charge of an unjust rule, you will enter their worldly life, away from a just imam. And in the sense of "if you turn away" through punishment, exile, and the thwarting of the Arabs in their jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) and their practice of raids and their persistence in them, then if its fruit is corruption in the land and the severing of kinship. It was also said its meaning is: if the people take charge of you and God hands you over to them. The most evident view is that this is an address to the hypocrites concerning the matter of fighting, which is what the preceding verses were about, meaning: if you turn away from complying with God's command regarding fighting.

﴿That you cause corruption in the land﴾ by not helping the people of Islam; when you do not help them, you sever the ties of kinship between you and them. This is indicated by ﴿those whom God has cursed﴾. So all the verses are about the hypocrites. This expectation expressed by "asa" is not attributed to Him, the Exalted, because He knows what was and what will be; it is rather relative to those who know the hypocrites, as if He says to them: "We have knowledge from the vantage of their loss: Is it to be expected from you, if you turn away from fighting, that such and such will happen?" The majority read ﴿tuqatti'u﴾ with doubled tashdid for intensification; Abu Amr, in one narration, Sallam, Ya'qub, Aban and Isma: with a single tashdid, the imperfect of qata'a; al-Hasan read "wa-taqattaʿu," with a fatha on the ta' and the qaf, dropping the preposition, meaning "your kinships," because taqattaʿa is intransitive. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those in whose hearts is a disease; ﴿so He deafened them﴾ to hearing the admonition; ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ to the path of guidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: God cursed them for their corruption and their severing of kinship, so He withheld His kindnesses from them and forsook them until they were blinded. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). The construction came as ﴿fa-asammahum﴾ (so He deafened them) and did not come as "fa-asamma adhanahum" (deafened their ears); and it came as ﴿wa-a'mā abṣārahum﴾ (and blinded their eyes) and did not come as "wa-a'amahum" (blinded them). It was said: because if the ear were deafened it would not perceive sight; the eye has a role in seeing and the ear has a role in hearing. End of quotation. For this reason it came as ﴿and upon their hearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 7], and ﴿and made for you hearing﴾, and it did not come as "and upon their ears," nor "and made for you ears."

When the ear was mentioned, heaviness (waqr) was attributed to it, which is less than deafness, as He said: ﴿and in our ears is heaviness﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an?﴾: that is, do they not examine it and what it contains of admonitions, warnings, and threats against the disobedient? This is an interrogative of rebuke and confrontation directed at those who fight against it.

﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ This is a metaphor for those among them in whom there is faith. ʾAm (or) here is disjunctive, meaning "rather"; the hamza is interrogative for affirmation. It is not impossible for them that their hearts are locked, so that no reminder reaches them. The description of the hearts did not require definition, because it is known that they are the hearts of those mentioned. There is no need to estimate an omitted attribute, that is, "or upon hearts whose locks are hard." He attributed the locks to them, meaning the particular locks, or they are the locks of unbelief that were shut so that they cannot be opened. It was read "iqfaluha" with a kasra on the hamza, which is a verbal noun, and "aqfuluha" in the plural pattern af'ul.

﴿Indeed those who turned back upon their heels after guidance had become clear to them﴾. Qatada said: It was revealed concerning a group of Jews who knew the matter of the Messenger from the Torah, and guidance became clear to them in this way; but when they came into contact with his affair they envied him, and they turned back from that measure of guidance. Ibn Abbas and others said: It was revealed concerning hypocrites who had become Muslim, then their hearts died. The verse encompasses everyone who enters within the scope of its wording.

Earlier, the discussion of *sawwala* (سَوَّلَ) was given in the commentary on Surah Yusuf. al-Zamakhshari said: "*sawwala lahum* means he made the committing of great sins seem attractive to them. It derives from *al-sawl*, which means slackness, and whoever derives it from *al-su'l* (request) has no knowledge of morphology (*al-tasrif*) or derivation (*al-ishtiqaq*) at all." End of quote. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "It has the meaning of *wa-la hum min al-sawl*, which means slackness and dangling." Others said: *sawwalahum* means "he gave them false hope" (*rajjahum*). Ibn Bahr said: "He gave them what they asked for" (*aʿtahum suʾlahum*).

al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and he derived it from..." to the end of his words, is not sound, because he assumed that the root of *al-sul* is the hamza. The two roots are different: either the root of *sawwala* is *w* and the middle radical of *al-suʾl* is a hamza, or the word *al-sul* has two roots: one with hamza, from *sa'ala yas'alu* (to ask), and the other with waw, from *sala yasalu* (to flow). If that is so, *sawwala* may be from the hamza-root. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: "*Al-taswil* originally comes from relaxing (*al-irkha'*), and from it is the verse ﴿فَدَلّاهُما بِغُرُورٍ﴾ (So he lowered them by deception) [al-Araf: 22]. *Al-sawl* is the slackening of the belly."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿سَوَّلَ لَهُمْ﴾ as *kaydahu* (his scheme), with an omitted noun (*mudaf*) assumed.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وأمْلى لَهُمْ﴾ with the verb in the active voice (*mabniyyan lil-fa'il*). The apparent meaning is that the subject refers to Satan. This was also said by al-Hasan, who understood his false promise of survival as a form of granting life (*al-ibqaʾ*). *Al-ibqaʾ* is survival for a long period of time, with extended hopes and wishes given to them.

It was said that the subject of *amla* may be a pronoun referring to God, and this is the more preferred view, because the true meaning of *al-imla'* (granting respite) belongs to God.

Ibn Sirin, al-Jahdari, Shayba, Abu ʿAmr and ʿIsa read *wa-umliya* in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ul*), meaning they were given respite and their lives were extended.

Mujahid, Ibn Hurmuz, al-Aʿmash, Sallam and Yaʿqub read *wa-umli* with the first-person hamza (*hamzat al-mutakallim*), as the present tense of *amla*, meaning "and I give them respite," like God's words ﴿إنَّما نُمْلِي لَهُمْ﴾ (We only give them respite) [Al ʿImran: 178]. It may also be a past tense in which the *ya'* has been dropped, as you would say *yaʿi* with a silent *ya'*.

﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم قالُوا لِلَّذِينَ كَرِهُوا ما نَزَّلَ﴾ (That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down). It is narrated that a group from Qurayza and al-Nadir used to help the hypocrites in opposing the Messenger and in working against him by supporting and aiding them. This is the meaning of His words ﴿سَنُطِيعُكم في بَعْضِ الأمْرِ﴾ (We will obey you in some of the matter).

It was also said: the pronoun in *qalu* refers to the hypocrites, and "those who hated what God had sent down" are Qurayza and al-Nadir. "Some of the matter" is the hypocrites' statement to them: ﴿لَئِنْ أُخْرِجْتُمْ لَنَخْرُجَنَّ مَعَكُمْ﴾ (If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you) [al-Hashr: 11]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

And the saying of al-Siddiq to al-Hasan, may God be pleased with them both: "Awla laka" (Woe to you!). End of quotation.

Most of them hold that ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾ is an independent sentence from which one of the two parts is omitted: either the predicate, whose implied form is "more fitting," which is the view of Mujahid and the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil; or the subject, whose implied form is "the matter is" or "we command obedience," that is, the matter pleasing to God is obedience. It was also said: it is a quotation of their words, that is, they said "obedience," and the reading of Ubayy supports this: "They say: obedience and fair speech." Their saying this was by way of mockery and deception. Qatada said: whoever stops at ﴿so woe to them, obedience﴾ begins a new sentence with the predicate, and the meaning is that this was from them by way of deception. It was also said: "obedience" is an attribute of "sura," meaning "so it is obedience," that is, something obeyed. This view is worthless because of the long separation between the attribute and the thing described.

﴿But when the matter is resolved﴾: that is, it becomes serious. ʿAzm means earnestness, and it belongs to the people of the matter. It is used metaphorically for the matter itself, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Surely that is among the steadfast matters﴾ [al-Shura: 43]. The poet said:

*War has become earnest with them, so they became earnest.*

The apparent answer to "idha" (when) is His saying: ﴿then if they had been true to God﴾, just as you say: "When it is winter, then if you come to me I will clothe you." It was also said: the answer is omitted, and its implied form is: "when the matter is resolved, it is so-and-so, or the like," as Qatada said. Whoever takes "obedience and fair speech" to mean that they say it by way of deception estimates the omitted answer as "the matter is resolved, let them be taken to account and pressed." Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "then I would believe," so ﴿if they had been true to God﴾ in what they claimed of their eagerness for jihad, or in their faith, and their hearts had agreed with their tongues on it, or in their hearts, ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾.

﴿Then, would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption in the land and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ The phrase ﴿so would you perhaps﴾ is a shift (iltifat) toward those in whose hearts is a disease; He turned to them with direct address by way of rebuke and to make them confront the evil of their conduct. The disagreement over the usage of "asa" (perhaps) has already been discussed. Concerning its reading when a second-person pronoun is attached to it in the sura al-Baqara, the attachment of the pronoun to it is the usage of the Hijaz, while the Banu Tamim do not attach the pronoun to it. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: They have mentioned that "asa" takes attached pronouns of both the nominative and accusative, and that it does not take the pronoun ... And as for the saying of whoever said "asa anta taqum" (perhaps you stand) and "asa ana aqum" (perhaps I stand), it is beneath what has been mentioned, a lengthy point with what it contains. End of quotation. I know of no one among the transmitters of Arabic who mentioned the separate pronoun after "asa," and it is separated between "asa" and its predicate by the condition, which is ﴿if you turn away﴾.

The majority read ﴿if you turn away﴾, meaning if you turn away from Islam. Qatada said: How did you see the people when they turned away from the Book of God? Did they not shed forbidden blood, sever the ties of kinship, and disobey the Merciful? He refers to what happened during the interval (fatra) after the time of the Messenger. Ka'b, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Aliya and al-Kalbi said: ﴿if you turn away﴾ means if you take charge of people's affairs through rule, and the reading "wulliitum" (passive) supports this. On this view it was said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayya. From the Prophet ﷺ: "in tawallaytum," with a damma on the ta' and the waw and a kasra on the lam, and with this reading ʿAli and Uways recited, meaning: if I put you in charge of an unjust rule, you will enter their worldly life, away from a just imam. And in the sense of "if you turn away" through punishment, exile, and the thwarting of the Arabs in their jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) and their practice of raids and their persistence in them, then if its fruit is corruption in the land and the severing of kinship. It was also said its meaning is: if the people take charge of you and God hands you over to them. The most evident view is that this is an address to the hypocrites concerning the matter of fighting, which is what the preceding verses were about, meaning: if you turn away from complying with God's command regarding fighting.

﴿That you cause corruption in the land﴾ by not helping the people of Islam; when you do not help them, you sever the ties of kinship between you and them. This is indicated by ﴿those whom God has cursed﴾. So all the verses are about the hypocrites. This expectation expressed by "asa" is not attributed to Him, the Exalted, because He knows what was and what will be; it is rather relative to those who know the hypocrites, as if He says to them: "We have knowledge from the vantage of their loss: Is it to be expected from you, if you turn away from fighting, that such and such will happen?" The majority read ﴿tuqatti'u﴾ with doubled tashdid for intensification; Abu Amr, in one narration, Sallam, Ya'qub, Aban and Isma: with a single tashdid, the imperfect of qata'a; al-Hasan read "wa-taqattaʿu," with a fatha on the ta' and the qaf, dropping the preposition, meaning "your kinships," because taqattaʿa is intransitive. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those in whose hearts is a disease; ﴿so He deafened them﴾ to hearing the admonition; ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ to the path of guidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: God cursed them for their corruption and their severing of kinship, so He withheld His kindnesses from them and forsook them until they were blinded. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). The construction came as ﴿fa-asammahum﴾ (so He deafened them) and did not come as "fa-asamma adhanahum" (deafened their ears); and it came as ﴿wa-a'mā abṣārahum﴾ (and blinded their eyes) and did not come as "wa-a'amahum" (blinded them). It was said: because if the ear were deafened it would not perceive sight; the eye has a role in seeing and the ear has a role in hearing. End of quotation. For this reason it came as ﴿and upon their hearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 7], and ﴿and made for you hearing﴾, and it did not come as "and upon their ears," nor "and made for you ears."

When the ear was mentioned, heaviness (waqr) was attributed to it, which is less than deafness, as He said: ﴿and in our ears is heaviness﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

﴿Do they not then ponder the Qur'an?﴾: that is, do they not examine it and what it contains of admonitions, warnings, and threats against the disobedient? This is an interrogative of rebuke and confrontation directed at those who fight against it.

﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ This is a metaphor for those among them in whom there is faith. ʾAm (or) here is disjunctive, meaning "rather"; the hamza is interrogative for affirmation. It is not impossible for them that their hearts are locked, so that no reminder reaches them. The description of the hearts did not require definition, because it is known that they are the hearts of those mentioned. There is no need to estimate an omitted attribute, that is, "or upon hearts whose locks are hard." He attributed the locks to them, meaning the particular locks, or they are the locks of unbelief that were shut so that they cannot be opened. It was read "iqfaluha" with a kasra on the hamza, which is a verbal noun, and "aqfuluha" in the plural pattern af'ul.

﴿Indeed those who turned back upon their heels after guidance had become clear to them﴾. Qatada said: It was revealed concerning a group of Jews who knew the matter of the Messenger from the Torah, and guidance became clear to them in this way; but when they came into contact with his affair they envied him, and they turned back from that measure of guidance. Ibn Abbas and others said: It was revealed concerning hypocrites who had become Muslim, then their hearts died. The verse encompasses everyone who enters within the scope of its wording.

Earlier, the discussion of *sawwala* (سَوَّلَ) was given in the commentary on Surah Yusuf. al-Zamakhshari said: "*sawwala lahum* means he made the committing of great sins seem attractive to them. It derives from *al-sawl*, which means slackness, and whoever derives it from *al-su'l* (request) has no knowledge of morphology (*al-tasrif*) or derivation (*al-ishtiqaq*) at all." End of quote. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "It has the meaning of *wa-la hum min al-sawl*, which means slackness and dangling." Others said: *sawwalahum* means "he gave them false hope" (*rajjahum*). Ibn Bahr said: "He gave them what they asked for" (*aʿtahum suʾlahum*).

al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and he derived it from..." to the end of his words, is not sound, because he assumed that the root of *al-sul* is the hamza. The two roots are different: either the root of *sawwala* is *w* and the middle radical of *al-suʾl* is a hamza, or the word *al-sul* has two roots: one with hamza, from *sa'ala yas'alu* (to ask), and the other with waw, from *sala yasalu* (to flow). If that is so, *sawwala* may be from the hamza-root. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: "*Al-taswil* originally comes from relaxing (*al-irkha'*), and from it is the verse ﴿فَدَلّاهُما بِغُرُورٍ﴾ (So he lowered them by deception) [al-Araf: 22]. *Al-sawl* is the slackening of the belly."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿سَوَّلَ لَهُمْ﴾ as *kaydahu* (his scheme), with an omitted noun (*mudaf*) assumed.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وأمْلى لَهُمْ﴾ with the verb in the active voice (*mabniyyan lil-fa'il*). The apparent meaning is that the subject refers to Satan. This was also said by al-Hasan, who understood his false promise of survival as a form of granting life (*al-ibqaʾ*). *Al-ibqaʾ* is survival for a long period of time, with extended hopes and wishes given to them.

It was said that the subject of *amla* may be a pronoun referring to God, and this is the more preferred view, because the true meaning of *al-imla'* (granting respite) belongs to God.

Ibn Sirin, al-Jahdari, Shayba, Abu ʿAmr and ʿIsa read *wa-umliya* in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ul*), meaning they were given respite and their lives were extended.

Mujahid, Ibn Hurmuz, al-Aʿmash, Sallam and Yaʿqub read *wa-umli* with the first-person hamza (*hamzat al-mutakallim*), as the present tense of *amla*, meaning "and I give them respite," like God's words ﴿إنَّما نُمْلِي لَهُمْ﴾ (We only give them respite) [Al ʿImran: 178]. It may also be a past tense in which the *ya'* has been dropped, as you would say *yaʿi* with a silent *ya'*.

﴿ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم قالُوا لِلَّذِينَ كَرِهُوا ما نَزَّلَ﴾ (That is because they said to those who hated what God had sent down). It is narrated that a group from Qurayza and al-Nadir used to help the hypocrites in opposing the Messenger and in working against him by supporting and aiding them. This is the meaning of His words ﴿سَنُطِيعُكم في بَعْضِ الأمْرِ﴾ (We will obey you in some of the matter).

It was also said: the pronoun in *qalu* refers to the hypocrites, and "those who hated what God had sent down" are Qurayza and al-Nadir. "Some of the matter" is the hypocrites' statement to them: ﴿لَئِنْ أُخْرِجْتُمْ لَنَخْرُجَنَّ مَعَكُمْ﴾ (If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you) [al-Hashr: 11]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It was also said: "some of the matter" means denying the Messenger, or denying *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God), or abandoning fighting alongside him.

It was said: it is the statement of both groups, the Jews and the hypocrites, to the polytheists: "We will obey you in agreeing to be hostile to the Messenger and in staying away from struggle (*jihad*) alongside him." *Fi ba'd al-amr* is specified as "in some of what they conceal," or "in some of the matter that concerns you."

The majority of reciters read *asrarahum* with a hamza that has a fatha. Their secrets were many. Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-Aʿmash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with a kasra on the hamza (*bi-kasriha*), which is a verbal noun (*masdar*). They said that this was said secretly among themselves, and God revealed it to them.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: "The more apparent reading is that God knows their secrets, which is what is in their hearts of knowledge of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). They were stubborn and arrogant, and they knew the Messenger of God (ﷺ) as they knew their own sons." End of quote.

﴿فَكَيْفَ إذا تَوَفَّتْهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (So how will it be when the angels take them at death?). The explanation of "those in whose hearts is a disease" has already been given, along with their reason for fighting. The statement of the apostates (*al-murtaddin*), and what awaits them of recompense for following the lies (*tawa'iyat al-kadhibin*) of what God has sent down, has also been given. And ﴿واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ إسْرارَهُمْ﴾ (and God knows their secrets) has been given. So this question, whose meaning is to make them aware (*al-tawqif*), comes after these things.

al-Tabari said: "So how is His knowledge of them, that is, of their secrets, when the angels take them at death?" It was also said: "So how will their condition be with God regarding what they committed of that statement?"

al-Aʿmash read *tawaffahum* with an alif in place of the taʾ. This may be either a past tense or a present tense with the taʾ omitted. The apparent meaning is that the time of death is the time of the taking of souls (*al-tawaffi*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "No one dies in a state of disobedience except that the angels strike his face and his back." The angels here are the Angel of Death and his assistants. It was also said: it is the time of fighting in support of the Messenger; they strike their faces so that they stand firm, and their backs so that they flee. *Al-malaʾika* here means "the help." The apparent meaning is that *yadribun* (striking) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-malaʾika*. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *tawaffahum*, but this is weak.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That): that is, that striking of faces and backs, ﴿بِأنَّهُمُ اتَّبَعُوا ما أسْخَطَ اللَّهَ﴾ (because they followed what angered God), which is disbelief, or concealing the sending of the Messenger, or Satan's enticement. These are several views. The one who follows something turns his face toward it, so it fits that the angels strike his face.

﴿وكَرِهُوا رِضْوانَهُ﴾ (and they disliked His pleasure): which is faith in God and following His religion. The disbeliever turns away from something, so it fits that the angels strike his back. In this there is a matching of two things with two things.

(p. 81) The believers were eager for the triumph of Islam, the exaltation of its word, and the wish to kill the enemy. They found companionship in revelation and felt lonely when it was delayed. God, the Exalted, has made this a fixed gate and an established rule that may not be transgressed. So God praised the believers for their request that a sura be sent down, and the meaning includes Our command to fight the enemy and to expose the hypocrites. Apparently those who made this request were sincere in their faith, and for this reason He said afterwards, ﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: They claimed eagerness for jihad and wished for it with their tongues, and they said, ﴿Why has a sura not been sent down?﴾ meaning concerning jihad.

﴿But when a sura is sent down﴾, and they were commanded in it to do what they had wished for and longed for, they recoiled, it was hard for them, and they were dismayed, like His saying: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. End of quotation. In this there is a warning contained in the wording of the Qur'an. And (lawla) means "why not" (hal-la). Abu Malik said: (la) is superfluous, and the construction is "if a sura were sent down," but this is nothing. It was read as "fa-idha nazalat" (when it descended). Zayd ibn Ali read "sura muhkama" with the accusative in both words, and the nominative of nuzzilat is pronounced with a damma, and "sura" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). He and Ibn Umar read "wa-dhukira" in the active voice, meaning God.

﴿Therein fighting is mentioned﴾. The majority read "sura muhkama" in the nominative, as the subject of a passive verb, and "dhukira" in the passive, with "al-qital" (fighting) as its substitute subject. Its being "muhkama" means that it is not abrogated. Qatada said: Every sura in which there is fighting is muhkama among the Qur'an, not specifically this verse, because fighting abrogated what had been truce and reconciliation, and it is not abrogated until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: muhkama means containing lawful and unlawful. It was also said: muhkama means that the literal meanings of its words are intended, as opposed to the mutashabih (ambiguous) in which a figurative sense is intended, such as His saying: ﴿The Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], ﴿in what I neglected concerning God﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], ﴿so strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4].

﴿You see those in whose hearts is a disease, looking at you﴾: that is, their eyes stare from cowardice and terror.

﴿With the look of one fainting from death﴾: that is, a look like that of one who has been overcome by a faint because death has come upon him. It was also said: they do this, which is a fixed stare at the Messenger out of intense enmity. It was also said: out of fear of exposure, for if they hold back from fighting they will be disgraced and their hypocrisy will be made manifest. ﴿Woe to them﴾: its explanation has already been given in al-Mufradat (Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary). Qatada said: as if He said, "Punishment is more fitting for them." It was also said: they are the disliked. Its morphological pattern is afalu or aflu, according to the disagreement, because istif'al, which we mentioned in al-Mufradat [applies]. According to the view of the majority, it is a noun that is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "for them." It was also said: awla is the subject, "for them" is its complement, and "obedience" is the predicate; it is as if the lam has the sense of the ba': "so fitting for them is obedience." Al-Zamakhshari did not address its i'rab (grammatical analysis), but said: its meaning is a supplication against them, that what they dislike should befall them. According to al-Asma'i's view, it is a verb whose subject is an implied pronoun understood from the meaning; it is omitted because of frequency of use, as if he said: "it has approached them," that is, destruction. Ibn Atiyya said: The well-known usage of the Arabs is only "awla laka," alone, by way of ellipsis and abbreviation, because of the strength it carries; so one says, as a rebuke and threat: "Awla laka, O so-and-so." This verse is of this type. From it is His saying: "Awla laka fa-awla" (Woe to you, and then woe!).
